136: I pay homage to the Buddha. I pay homage to the well-expounded Dhamma. I pay homage to the Saṅgha of good conduct. This discourse beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Bākula Sutta. In this Bākula Sutta, the meaning of the term 'Bākula' should be understood as follows: Just as people in the world speak of 'twenty-two' (bāvīsati) and 'thirty-three' (bāttiṃsa), he is called 'Bākula' because he is said to be of 'two families' (dvikula). I shall now relate the story of that Elder Bākula. That Elder had previously belonged to two families. Having passed away from the celestial realm, the Elder Bākula was reborn into the family of a great merchant in the city of Kosambī. On the fifth day, they performed the head-washing ceremony for the child and took him to play in the river Gaṅgā. While the nurses were letting the child play by dipping him in and out of the water, a fish saw the child and, thinking 'This is my food,' it opened its mouth and approached. The nurses abandoned the child and fled. That fish swallowed the child. The meritorious child did not suffer any pain but felt as if he had entered a bedchamber and was lying down. Due to the child's merit, the fish felt as if it had swallowed a hot frying pan; being greatly distressed, it swam swiftly for a distance of thirty yojanas and entered the net of a fisherman living in the city of Vārāṇasī. Usually, large fish die when they are caught in a net and struck, but this fish died only after being taken out of the net, due to the child's power. Although fishermen usually cut open and sell large fish when they catch them, due to the child's power, they did not cut this fish but carried it whole on a pole, wandering through the city saying, 'We will sell this for a thousand pieces of money.' No one bought it. In that city, there was a merchant family with a wealth of eighty crores who had no children. When the fishermen reached the door of that house and were asked, 'For how much will you give it?', they replied, 'For a thousand kahāpaṇas.' The merchants paid the money and bought it. Although the merchant's wife did not usually care for fish on other days, on that day she placed the fish on a board and cut it open herself. While fish are normally cut from the belly, she cut it from the back; seeing the golden-hued child inside the fish's belly, she cried out, 'I have obtained a son from the belly of a fish!' and taking the child, she went to her husband, the merchant. The merchant immediately had the drums beaten and, taking the child, went to the King and said, 'Great King, I have obtained a child from the belly of a fish; what should I do?' The King replied, 'This child who could live in a fish's belly without illness is one of great merit; raise him.' The other family heard that 'a merchant family in Vārāṇasī has obtained a child from the belly of a fish' and went there. When the child's [original] mother saw the child adorned and playing, she said, 'This child is truly delightful,' and approaching, she told the whole story. The second mother said, 'This child is my son.' When asked, 'Where did you get him?', she replied, 'From the belly of a fish.' The first mother said, 'He is not your son, he is only my son.' When asked, 'Where did you get him?', she explained, 'I carried him in my womb for ten months, and then while letting him play in the river, a fish swallowed him.' The other replied, 'Another fish might have swallowed your son, but this child was obtained from the belly of a large fish.' Thus they disputed and both went to the King's palace. The King said, 'Since this woman carried him in her womb for ten months, it cannot be said she is not the mother. Since this woman who bought the fish obtained him from the fish's belly—and no one catches a fish by removing its entrails beforehand—it cannot be said she is not the mother either. Therefore, let the child be the heir to both families, and both of you shall care for him.' Thus, both families cared for him. When he reached the age of discretion...
137: ...while playing in the river, a fish swallowed him. 'Your son must have been swallowed by another fish, but I obtained this child from the belly of this fish,' they said, and both went to the royal palace. The King said, 'Because this woman carried him in her womb for ten months, she cannot be dismissed as the mother. Since there is no one who catches a fish by first removing its entrails, this woman who obtained him from the fish's belly also cannot be dismissed as the mother. Let the child be the heir to both families; both of you should look after him.' So both families cared for him. When he reached the age of maturity, they had palaces built for him in both cities and provided him with troupes of dancers. He lived for four months in each city. When he had completed four months in one city and was to move to the other, they would set up a pavilion and place him there along with the dancers. Enjoying such prosperity, he would travel to the other city. The residents of that city would come halfway to meet him with dancers. They would greet him, surround him, and lead him to their own palace. The dancers who had come from the other city would then turn back and return to their own city. After staying there for four months, he would return to the other city in the same manner. In this way, enjoying such prosperity, he reached eighty years of age. Then, the Blessed One, while wandering on a walking tour, arrived at Vārāṇasī. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, he gained faith and was ordained. After ordaining, he remained a worldling (puthujjana) for only seven days, and on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus, he had two families. For that reason, he came to be known as 'Bākula.' 'Purāṇagihisahāyo' means a companion from his former life as a layman. This Acela Kassapa was also long-lived, and when he went to see the Elder Bākula after his ordination, he was already eighty years old. By the phrase 'methuno dhammo' (sexual intercourse), the foolish naked ascetic (Acela Kassapa) was asking a foolish question; it was not a matter concerning the Dispensation (Sāsana). Now, standing in the method provided by the Elder, he asked, 'By these things, your...' The words beginning with 'yampāyasmā' were established and fixed in all sections by the Elders who conducted the Dhamma Council (Dhammasaṅgāhaka). In that context, it should be understood that perception (saññā) is merely what has arisen, while thought (vitakka) performs the differentiation of the pathways of action (kammapatha).
138:
The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, however, said: "Why do they do them separately? Both of these (perception and thought) are indeed destroyers of the path of action (kammapatha)."

"Gahapaticīvara" refers to the robes offered to monks who have completed the rains retreat. "Satthena" means (cutting) with a knife. "Sucitā" means he does not remember (it never happened) having ever sewn while holding a needle. "Kathinacīvara" refers to the Kathina robe; since the Kathina robe is also categorized as a rains-residence robe, he said regarding that Kathina robe as well, "I do not remember sewing it."

Regarding where the Venerable Bākula obtained robes during all this time when he did not delight in robes offered by lay devotees and did not perform cutting or sewing—he obtained them from two cities (Kosambī and Vārāṇasī). The Elder Bākula had a great following and fame; his children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren would have robes made from fine cloth, dyed, placed in caskets, and sent to him. When the Elder bathed, they would place them in the bathhouse. The Elder would wear those new robes and give the old robes to any newly ordained monks who arrived. After wearing those robes, the Elder did not perform any new work; there was no task whatsoever for him to strive for. He dwelt only by repeatedly entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). When about four months had passed and the robes became soiled, they would send them again in the same manner. Some teachers even say he changed and wore them every fortnight.

This is not a wonder for the Elder of great merit and great super-knowledge (abhiññā), who fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons. The Elder Nigrodha, the spiritual advisor to King Asoka the Righteous, changed his robes three times a day. For that Elder, three robes were placed on the back of an elephant and brought early in the morning along with five hundred perfume caskets and five hundred flower caskets; likewise at noon and in the evening. It is said that the King, when changing his own clothes three times a day, would ask, "Have the robes been taken for the Elder?" and only upon hearing "Yes, they have been taken," would he change his own. The Elder also did not tie them into bundles and store them, but gave them to any fellow celibates (sabrahmacārī) who arrived. It is said that at that time, the majority of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha in Jambudīpa possessed robes that had belonged to the Elder Nigrodha.

Is it difficult not to give rise to the thought, "If only someone would invite me," or is it difficult to abandon such a thought once it has arisen? Since the mind is something that changes quickly, preventing such a thought from arising is...
139:
...difficult, and abandoning it once it has arisen is also difficult. "Antaraghare" (inside the house/village) in the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta is said to be from the threshold pillar inwards, but in this Bākula Sutta, it is intended to mean the place where the eaves-drop falls. From where did Venerable Bākula receive alms? The Venerable was very famous in the two cities, and when he arrived at a house door, the householders would take the Venerable's bowl, fill it with various delicious foods, and offer it. He would return from the place where he received alms; his place for taking meals was also permanently fixed. "Anubyañjanaso" means the Venerable never looked at a woman by taking note of her features in her form. "Mātugāmassa dhammaṃ" means it is allowable to preach the Dhamma to a woman with five or six words; if questioned, it is even allowable to speak as many as a thousand verses. However, the Venerable did not do so, even though it was allowable. Indeed, such an action is mostly the work of elders who frequent the houses of lay devotees. "Bhikkhunupassayaṃ" refers to the quarters of the bhikkhunīs. Although it is allowable to go to that quarters to inquire after the sick, the Venerable did not do so, even though it was allowable. This principle should be understood in all instances. "Cuṇṇena" refers to powder made from Kosamba powder and so on. "Gattaparikamma" refers to the act of massaging the body. "Vicāritā" refers to the one who causes (someone else) to do it. "Gaddūhanamattaṃ" refers to the time it takes to hold a cow's teat and squeeze out one drop of milk.

For what reason was Venerable Bākula free from illness? It is said that when the Blessed One Padumuttara was wandering with a retinue of a hundred thousand monks, poisonous trees bloomed in the Himalayas. At that time, the disease called tiṇapupphaka broke out among the hundred thousand monks. At that time, the Venerable was an ascetic with psychic powers; while traveling through the air, he saw the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, descended, inquired about the illness, and brought medicinal roots from the Himalayas and offered them. By merely smelling that medicine, the illness was subsided. Also, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, on the first day of sowing, he set aside his own sowing work and built a fire room and a toilet for the use of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, and regularly offered medicinal requirements. Due to this meritorious deed, he became free from illness. This Venerable Bākula was one who practiced the strict sitting-up dhutanga (nesajjika) and the strict forest-dwelling dhutanga (āraññaka). Therefore, the Venerable said such words as "I do not know of having leaned against a support when there was no support to lean on." "Saraṇo" means being with defilements. "Aññā udapādi" means it is not proper to declare one's attainment of Arahantship to one who is not ordained. If so, why did the Venerable declare it? Because the Venerable did not directly say "I am an Arahant," but only said "The knowledge of Arahantship has arisen." Alternatively, he said this because it was already well-known that the Venerable was an Arahant.
140:
The Elder Bākula did not personally perform the novice ordination (pabbajjā) or the higher ordination (upasampadā), but had other monks do so. "Taking the key" means holding the key-block. "He attained Parinibbāna while sitting" means he reflected, "While I was alive, I was not a burden to other monks; even after I have attained Parinibbāna, let my body not be an encumbrance to the Saṅgha of monks." Thus, he entered the fire element (tejodhātu) and attained Parinibbāna. At that time, flames emerged from his body, and the skin, flesh, and blood were consumed like ghee until they were gone. Only relics (dhātu) resembling jasmine buds remained. The rest of the account is well-known in all versions. This Bākula Sutta was chanted during the Second Council.

## Within the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Bākula Sutta is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Dantabhūmi Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Dantabhūmi Sutta. In that sutta, "in a forest hut" refers to a dwelling made for monks who practice meditation in a secluded part of that very Veḷuvana monastery. "Prince" refers to Prince Jayasena, the biological son of King Bimbisāra. "Would attain" means he might obtain. "One-pointedness" means he says, "I have heard that one who practices in this way obtains attainment (samāpatti), obtains meditative absorption (jhāna)." "Fatigue" refers to physical fatigue. "Distress" refers to that same fatigue. "Stay within your own range" means stay only within the scope of what you do not know.

"He taught" means he taught the preliminary practice of the kasina (kasiṇa-parikamma), leading up to access concentration (upacāra) and fixed concentration (appanā), explaining that one-pointedness of mind can be obtained in this way, and attainment can be produced in this way. "Having shown" means having made it clear. "To be known through renunciation (nekkhamma)" means it should be known through the quality of having emerged from sensual pleasures. This was taught with the meaning that a person established in the quality of having emerged from sensual pleasures knows one-pointedness.
141:
This was taught with such an intention. The remaining terms are merely synonyms for that statement. "Consuming sensual pleasures" (kāme paribhuñjanto) means enjoying both types of sensual pleasures (objective and subjective).
In the phrase "whether an elephant to be tamed, a horse to be tamed, or an ox to be tamed," here, persons lacking one-pointedness of mind should be seen as being like untamed elephants and so forth. Persons endowed with one-pointedness of mind should be seen as being like tamed elephants and so forth. Just as untamed elephants and so forth are unable to walk the path of tamed elephants or reach the place to be reached by tamed elephants without acting deceitfully and without abandoning their burden; even so, persons lacking one-pointedness of mind are unable to produce the special qualities produced by those endowed with one-pointedness of mind, nor can they reach the level that should be reached.
"Hatthavilaṅghakena" means holding hand by hand. "Daṭṭheyya" means something worthy of being looked at. "Āvuṭo" means obstructed. "Nivuṭo" means prevented. "Ophuṭo" means covered over.
"Nāgavanika" in the Hatthipadopama Sutta refers to a man who roams the elephant forest, but in this Dantabhūmi Sutta, it means a man skilled in elephant lore who is capable of capturing an elephant. "Atipassitvā" means having seen. "Etthagedhā" means the greed that arises in those elephant habitats. "Sarasaṅkappānaṃ" means thoughts of running about. In the phrase "for the sake of undertaking virtues pleasing to humans," when an elephant is played with by men, women, boys, and girls who hold its trunk and so forth, and that elephant remains pleasant without any abnormality, then that elephant is said to have undertaken the habits (sīla) pleasing to humans.
"Pemanīyā" refers to speech that elephants love and cherish, such as: "O noble elephant, the King is pleased with you and will place you in the position of the auspicious state elephant; you will receive food and such worthy of a king." "Sussūsati" means desiring to listen to that pleasant speech. "Tiṇaghāsodakaṃ" means grass and water. "Tiṇaghāsaṃ" means grass to be eaten, grass to be chewed.
"Paṇavo" means a small drum. "Sabbavaṅkadosanihitaninnītakasāvo" means having abandoned all faults of crookedness and having removed the stain of astringent impurity. "Aṅganteva saṅkhaṃ gacchati" means it reaches the state of being equal to a limb.
"Gehasitasīlānaṃ" refers to virtues based on the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Upāyassa" (in the Pali text, it is 'Ñāyassa') is the meaning of the Eightfold Path. "Adantamahallakāraññanāgo kālaṅkaroti" means the King's great forest elephant dies without being tamed.
142:
"Virtue based on the household" (gehasita-sīla) refers to virtues dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Ñāya" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path. "The king's large elephant died untamed" means the king's large elephant died without being tamed, it passed away; it performed the act of dying while untamed—this is the meaning here. This method applies everywhere. The rest is clear.

## Within the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Dantabhūmi Sutta is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Bhūmija Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Bhūmija Sutta. In that sutta, "Bhūmija" refers to this Elder Bhūmija, who was the maternal uncle of Prince Jayasena. "Longing and not longing" means longing at one time and not longing at another time. "With his own bowl of rice" means he served him with the alms-food normally received, as well as with the rice prepared for himself. In all places, the rest is clear.

## 7. Explanation of the Anuruddha Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Anuruddha Sutta. In that sutta, "thus they said" means they approached and spoke thus when that lay follower Pañcakaṅga was unwell. "Apaṇṇaka" means being without failure. "Ekattha" (of one meaning) refers to this: whether called "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) or "exalted" (mahaggata), it is only jhāna that is so called because of the one-pointedness of mind. It was said with reference to this meaning.
143:
The phrase "abiding by pervading an area the size of a single tree root with mahaggata jhāna" means overwhelming an area the size of a single tree root with the kasina sign (kasina-nimitta), and abiding by pervading and attending to the mahaggata jhāna within that kasina sign. For a person who does not attain jhāna, there is no such attention (ābhoga) as 'mahaggata'; this is said merely by way of the occurrence of mahaggata jhāna. This method should be understood in all cases. "By this reason, householder, it should be known" means for this cause. For, in this context, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) of the Brahma-vihāras, which are called 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa), does not expand, nor does the removal of the counterpart sign occur. Those jhānas do not serve as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) or for the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); rather, they serve only as the basis for insight (vipassanā), as the basis for the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and as a means for descending into a new existence (bhavokkamana). However, the counterpart sign of the kasina jhānas, which are called 'exalted' (mahaggata), does expand, its removal occurs, and the transcending of signs takes place. They serve as the basis for direct knowledge, the basis for the attainment of cessation, the basis for the round of rebirth, and as a means for descending into a new existence. Thus, these states differ in meaning, and they also differ in phrasing as 'immeasurable' and 'exalted'.

Now, wishing to show the cause of rebirth in a new existence after emerging from the mahaggata attainment, the Buddha said, "There are these four," and so on. For one who knows by pervading that "there is the realm of Limited Radiance (Parittābha)," there is this attention. Indeed, this is said with reference to a person who develops the jhāna that is the cause of rebirth among the Parittābha devas. This method should be understood in all cases. Some devas of Limited Radiance have defiled radiance (saṅkiliṭṭhābha), while some have pure radiance (parisuddhābha). Some devas of Immeasurable Radiance (Appamāṇābha) have defiled radiance, while some have pure radiance. How so? A person who performs the preliminary work (parikamma) on a kasina the size of a small offering-saucer or a bowl, produces an attainment, and has mastery (vasībhāva) practiced in five ways, but because the opposing states (hindrances) have not been well-cleansed, he makes use of a weak attainment. If he dies while established in that unpracticed jhāna, he is reborn in the realms of Limited Radiance; his appearance is both limited and defiled. However, a person who has mastery practiced in five ways, and because the opposing states have been well-cleansed, makes use of a very pure attainment. If he dies while established in that well-practiced jhāna, he is reborn in the realms of Limited Radiance; his appearance is limited but pure. In this way, some devas of Limited Radiance have defiled radiance, and some have pure radiance. The entire explanation regarding a person who performs extensive preliminary work on a kasina, produces an attainment, and has mastery practiced in five ways, should be understood in the same way as the previous method. Thus, some devas of Immeasurable Radiance have defiled radiance, and some have pure radiance.
144:
The term "diversity of appearance" (vaṇṇanānatta) refers to the diversity of the color of the body. "Not diversity of radiance" (no ca ābhānānatta) means that diversity in the light is not apparent. "Diversity of flame" (accinānatta) refers to the diversity of a lamp flame by way of being long, short, small, or large.

"Wherever" (yatta yatta) refers to wherever it may be—in gardens, mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, riverbanks, or on the banks of lotus ponds. "They settle" (abhinivisanti) means they dwell. "They delight" (abhiramanti) means they enjoy themselves without becoming weary. "By a carrying-pole" (kājena) means by any carrying-pole among those carrying gruel, rice, oil, molasses, fish, or meat. There is also a reading "kācena," which has the same meaning. "By a basket" (piṭakena) means by a wicker basket. "In that very place" (tattha tattheva) means that even if they are taken from a place where ghee, honey, molasses, etc., are easily available to a place where salty things and rotting fish are abundant, they do not give rise to thoughts such as, "Our former dwelling place was pleasant; we lived there happily; now in this place, the salt oppresses us, or the smell of rotting fish causes a headache." Instead, they delight only in those various places.

"Radiance" (ābhā) means being endowed with radiance. "By that factor" (tadangeṇa) means by way of the cause of rebirth in that realm. Now, wishing to ask about that cause, he said, "Who is it, venerable sir?" and so on.

"Bodily discomfort" (kāyaduṭṭhulla) refers to the state of bodily sluggishness. "From one meditating" (jhāyato) means from a burning lamp.

Regarding the words "For a long time, indeed, I..." (dīgharattaṃ kho me), it is said that while the Elder Anuruddha was fulfilling the perfections, he went forth as a hermit (isi), produced attainments, and subsequently obtained rebirth in the Brahma world for three hundred consecutive existences; this was said with reference to that. This has also been said:

"For three hundred existences without interruption, I went forth in the going-forth of a hermit;
Seeking the Unconditioned, that was my former wandering."

All the remaining words are clear in meaning.

## The explanation of the Anuruddha Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
## 8. Upakkilesasutta-vaṇṇanā

"Thus have I heard" and so on refers to the Upakkilesa Sutta. Therein, "he said this" was not said with the intention of causing a split, nor out of a desire to be liked, but rather because this thought occurred to that monk: "These quarreling Kosambaka monks will turn away from their dispute by taking my words. The Buddhas, indeed, desire the welfare of others and do not speak what is not the cause. The Blessed One will preach this matter to me. Having heard that teaching, those quarreling Kosambaka monks will turn away. Because of that turning away, there will be happy living for those monks." Thus, he spoke the words "That, venerable sir," and so on, out of a desire for their welfare. In the words "Do not [engage in] quarreling" (mā bhaṇḍanaṃ) and so on, the meaning should be understood by taking the rest of the Pali as "Do not perform quarreling." "A certain [monk]" (aññataro) refers to that undistinguished monk who desired the welfare of the Blessed One. His intention was: "These Kosambaka monks, who are overwhelmed by anger, are unable to follow the words of the Blessed One; let not the Blessed One be weary in disciplining those monks." Therefore, out of a desire for the Blessed One's welfare, he spoke the words "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is the Lord of Dhamma" and so on. "I walk for alms" (piṇḍāya carāmi) should be understood in detail.
145:
“These monks will not listen to my words and desist [from quarreling]. However, Buddhas are indeed compassionate and seek the welfare of beings; the Blessed One will surely teach them a certain reason. Upon hearing it, these monks will desist, and then they will live in comfort.” This was the thought. Therefore, he spoke the words beginning with, “Here, Bhante...” In the phrase “mā bhaṇḍanaṃ” and others, the remaining Pali word “akatthā” should be taken, and the meaning should be understood as “Do not engage in quarreling.” “Aññataro” refers to that certain monk who was well-wishing toward the Blessed One. His intention was: “These monks, overcome by anger, do not heed the Teacher’s words; let not the Blessed One be exhausted while admonishing these monks.” Thus, he spoke in this way.

Regarding the phrase “He entered for alms,” He did not merely enter; He also made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): “May those who have not yet seen me, see me.” For what purpose did He make this resolution? It was for the purpose of taming those monks. At that time, after returning from the alms round, the Blessed One recited the verses beginning with “Puthusaddo samajano” and departed from Kosambī for the village of Bālakaloṇakāra. From there, He went to the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park, and then to the Pālileyyaka forest thicket, where He stayed for the three months of the rainy season, being attended to by the noble elephant Pālileyyaka. The townspeople also thought, “The Teacher has arrived at the monastery; let us go to hear the Dhamma.” Carrying flowers and perfumes, they went to the monastery and asked, “Venerables, where is the Teacher?” The monks replied, “How can you see the Teacher now? The Teacher came thinking, ‘I will make these monks harmonious,’ but being unable to make them harmonious, He has departed.” The people said, “We could not bring the Teacher even by giving a hundred or a thousand pieces of wealth. Such a Teacher came of His own accord without our invitation, yet because of these monks, we have lost the opportunity to hear the Dhamma in the Teacher’s presence. These monks went forth dedicated to the Teacher, yet even when the Teacher Himself tried to create harmony, they did not become harmonious. Whose words will they listen to other than the Buddha’s? It is enough; alms should not be offered to these monks.” Thus, they imposed a penalty (boycott) throughout the entire city. On the following day, although those monks wandered for alms throughout the city, they did not receive even a spoonful of food and had to return to the monastery. The lay devotees said to them again, “As long as you do not ask the Teacher for forgiveness, this same penalty shall remain for you.” Then the monks thought, “We will ask the Teacher for forgiveness,” and when the Blessed One arrived at Sāvatthī, they went there. The Teacher then taught them the eighteen grounds for creating a schism (bhedakaravatthūni). This is the extra-canonical explanation (pāḷimuttaka-kathā) in this context.

Now, in the verses beginning with “Puthusaddo,” “Puthusaddo” means having a great noise. “Samajano” means having similar or equal companions. This means that this group of monks has a great noise due to the sounds of quarreling all around, and they are similar in their desire to quarrel. “Na bālo koci maññatha” means that not even a single one among those monks considers himself, “I am a fool”; instead, all of them conceive themselves to be wise (paṇḍitamānino). “Nāññaṃ bhiyyo maññare” means that not even one of those monks...
146:
The meaning is that the group of people who engage in quarreling is “of great noise” (puthusaddo) because they emit sounds all around, and they are “similar” (samajano) in their quarreling. “No one considers himself a fool” (na bālo koci maññatha) means that among them, not even a single one thinks, “I am a fool”; all of them indeed conceive themselves to be wise. “They do not consider any other reason further” (nāññaṃ bhiyyo amaññaruṃ) means that not even one thinks “I am a fool,” and while the Saṅgha is splitting, they do not consider this other reason: “The Saṅgha is splitting because of me.”

“Parimuṭṭhā” means those who are devoid of mindfulness (muṭṭhassatino). In the term “vācāgocarabhāṇino,” the syllable “rā” has been shortened. They speak only within the range of words (vācāgocara), not within the range of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānagocara). How do they speak? They speak by opening their mouths as much as they wish; not even one monk restrains his mouth (or contracts his face) out of respect for the Saṅgha. “Yena nītā” means that by which quarrel they have been led to this shameless state. “Na taṃ vidū” means they do not know that “there is such a danger (ādīnava) in this quarrel.” “Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti” means those who harbor such grudges as “He abused me,” and so on. “Sanantano” means an ancient tradition or law.

“Pare” means those other than the wise, namely the fools who engage in quarreling. While they are quarreling in the midst of the Saṅgha, they do not realize [with the perception of impermanence]: “We shall die, we shall perish, we are constantly and continuously approaching the presence of Death (yamāmase).” “Ye ca tattha vijānanti” means those wise monks among them who realize, “We are going near to Death.” “Tato sammanti medhagā” means that those wise monks, knowing thus and producing wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), practice for the stilling of quarrels (medhagā). The verse beginning with “Aṭṭhicchinnā” appears in the Jātaka and was spoken with reference to King Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu. The meaning here is: even for those who had such long-standing grudges that their parents’ bones were broken, reconciliation (sangati) was possible; why is it not possible for you, whose parents’ bones have not been broken, whose lives have not been taken, and whose cattle, horses, and wealth have not been plundered?
147:
The verse beginning with "Sace labhetha" was spoken to show the presence or absence of benefits in wise and foolish companions. "Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayāni" means that one should overcome manifest dangers such as lions, leopards, and tigers, as well as hidden dangers such as snakes, scorpions, and lice, and wander with that person, joyful and mindful.

"Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ" means that one should wander alone just as King Mahājanaka and King Arindama abandoned their conquered kingdoms and wandered alone. "Mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo" means "like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest." The word Mātaṅga refers to an elephant. Nāga is a designation for a great being. Just as the Mātaṅga elephant king, who cared for his mother, wandered alone in the forest and did no evil, and just as the Pālileyyaka elephant king wandered alone, so too should one wander alone and do no evil.

Bālakaloṇakāra village is the village granted for the enjoyment of the householder Upāli. "Tenupasaṅkami" (He approached there): Why did he approach? Because the Buddha, seeing the disadvantages in a group, felt a desire to see a monk who dwells alone. Therefore, like one oppressed by cold seeking heat, he approached. "Dhammiyā kathāyā" means with a talk related to the benefits of solitude. Why did he approach Pācīnavaṃsadāya? Because, having seen the disadvantages in quarreling monks, he felt a desire to see monks who dwell in harmony. Therefore, like one oppressed by cold seeking heat, he approached that place. "The venerable Anuruddha" and so on is as previously explained.

With the final question, "Atthi pana vo," he would ask about the supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma). However, since those elders did not yet possess supramundane states, he thought it inappropriate to ask about them and instead asked about the light produced by preliminary concentration (parikamma-samādhi). "Obhāsañceva sañjānāma" means "we perceive the light of preliminary concentration." "Dassanañca rūpānaṃ" means "we perceive the seeing of forms with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu)." "Tañca nimittaṃ nappaṭivijjhāma" means "we do not know the reason why the light and the seeing of forms disappear for us."

"Taṃ kho pana vo Anuruddhā nimittaṃ paṭivijjhita bbaṃ" means "Anuruddhas, you must know that cause." "Ahampi sudaṃ" was said to show, "Anuruddhas, why should I not be disturbed? I too was previously disturbed by these eleven defilements (upakkilesa)." This teaching...
148:
The Blessed One began the teaching. In the passages beginning with "Vicikicchā kho me," the Bodhisatta increased the light and, upon seeing various forms with the direct knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), indecisive doubt arose: "What is this object?" "Samādhi cavi" means the preliminary concentration fell away. "Obhāsa" means the light produced by preliminary concentration also disappeared, and he no longer saw forms with the divine eye. "Amanasikāra" (Non-attention) means while looking at forms, doubt arose, and then the thought "Now I will not attend to any object" occurred, and thus non-attention arose. When not attending to any object, sloth and torpor (thina-middha) arose.

"Chambhitatta" (Consternation) means when he increased the light towards the Himalayas, he saw Dānava demons, pythons, and so on, and then trembling of the body arose. "Uppila" (Elation) means manifest rapture (pīti) arose in the Bodhisatta as he thought, "When I look normally, there is nothing to fear. Why should I fear an object not yet seen?" "Sakideva" means that with only a single effort, one could see five large treasure pots.

"Duṭṭhulla" (Grossness) means he thought, "Because I exerted effort intensely, elation-rapture (uppila-pīti) arose," and so he relaxed his effort; then bodily distress, bodily grossness, and laziness arose. "Accāraddhavīriya" (Excessive effort) means he thought, "Because I relaxed my effort, grossness arose," and when he raised the effort again, excessive effort arose. "Patameyya" means "might die." "Atilīnavīriya" (Overly slack effort) means he thought, "When I increased my effort, this happened," and when he relaxed his effort again, overly slack effort arose.

"Abhijappā" (Longing) means craving (taṇhā) arose in the Bodhisatta as he increased the light towards the deva realm and looked at the hosts of devas. "Nānattasaññā" (Perception of diversity) means he thought, "When I attend to a form having a single nature, longing arises; I will attend to various objects," and as he increased the light sometimes towards the deva realm and sometimes towards the human realm, attending to various forms, the perception occurring in various modes arose. "Atinijjhāyitatta" (Excessive scrutiny) means he thought, "When I attend to various forms, the perception of diversity arises; whether it is desirable or undesirable, I will attend only to a form having a single nature," and as he did so, excessive scrutiny of forms arose.

"Obhāsanimittaṃ manasikaromi" means attending only to the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) produced by preliminary meditation. "Na ca rūpāni passāmi" means not seeing forms with the divine eye. "Rūpanimittaṃ pana manasikaromi" means attending only to the forms that are the objects of the divine eye. "Parittañceva obhāsaṃ" means perceiving the counterpart sign in a limited area, and "parittañca rūpāni" means seeing forms in a limited area. The second section, which is immeasurable (appamāṇa), should also be understood in the opposite way. "Parittaṃ samādhiṃ gahitosmi" refers to the counterpart sign produced by limited preliminary meditation.
149:
"I attend to the sign of light" (obhāsanimittaṃ manasi karomi) means attending only to the sign of light produced by preparatory meditation (parikamma-bhāvanā). "And I do not see forms" (na ca rūpāni passāmi) means not seeing visible objects with the divine-eye superknowledge (dibba-cakkhu-abhiññā). "I attend to the sign of forms" (rūpanimittaṃ manasi karomi) means attending only to the visible object that is the object of the divine-eye superknowledge.

"Limited light" (parittañceva obhāsaṃ) means knowing light in a limited place. "Limited forms" (parittāni ca rūpāni) means seeing forms in a limited place. The second round should be understood in reverse. "Limited concentration" (paritto samādhi) refers to limited preparatory light. Here, preparatory concentration is called "limited" with reference to the limitedness of the light. "Limited for me at that time" (parittaṃ me tasmiṃ samaye) means that at that time, the divine-eye superknowledge is also limited. The same method should be understood for the "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) section.

"Without initial application, but with sustained application only" (avitakkampi vicāramattaṃ) refers to the second jhāna concentration in the five-fold system. "Without initial application and without sustained application" (avitakkampi avicāraṃ) refers to the concentration of the group of three jhānas in both the four-fold and five-fold systems. "With rapture" (sappītikaṃ) refers to the concentration of the second and third jhānas. "Without rapture" (nippītikaṃ) refers to the concentration of the group of two jhānas. "Accompanied by pleasant feeling" (sātasahagataṃ) refers to concentration in the three-fold and four-fold systems. "Accompanied by equanimity" (upekkhāsahagataṃ) refers to the fourth jhāna concentration in the four-fold system and the fifth jhāna concentration in the five-fold system.

When did the Blessed One develop this three-fold concentration? He developed it in the last watch of the night while sitting at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree. The Blessed One's first path (magga) was of the first jhāna. The second path and others were of the second, third, and fourth jhānas. Since there is no path of the fifth jhāna in the five-fold system, that fifth jhāna was mundane (lokiya). This was taught with reference to the mixture of mundane and supramundane. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

## 9. Commentary on the Bālapandita Sutta
"Thus have I heard" (evaṃ me sutaṃ) and so forth refers to the Bālapandita Sutta. In that sutta, "characteristics of a fool" (bālalakkhaṇāni) are so called because a person is characterized or known as "this person is a fool" by these traits. Those same characteristics are called "signs of a fool" (bālanimittāni) because they are the cause for recognizing that fool. They are called "conduct of a fool" (bālapadānāni) because they are the fool's reasons/actions.
150:
The conduct of fools (bālapadānāni). "One who thinks bad thoughts" (duccintitacintī) means that when thinking, one thinks only bad thoughts by way of covetousness (abhijjhā), ill-will (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). "One who speaks bad words" (dubbhasitabhāsī) means that even when speaking, one speaks only bad words such as lying (musāvāda) and so forth. "One who does bad deeds" (dukkaṭakammakārī) means that even when acting, one performs only bad deeds by way of killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth. "And there" (tatra ca) means in that assembly where one is sitting. "Appropriate and suitable for him" (tajjaṃ tassāruppaṃ) means talk that is suitable and fitting for that fool, connected with the danger of the five enmities in the present life and the future life. "There" (tatra) means while that talk regarding the faults is being discussed. The words "the fool" (bālaṃ) and so forth are in the accusative case (upayoga) used in the sense of the genitive (sāmi).

"They hang down" (olambanti) means they appear (upaṭṭhahanti) at the time of death. The remaining two words (alambanti, abhisampanti) are synonyms of that word. Because those signs of action (kamma-nimitta) and signs of destination (gati-nimitta) appear by way of hanging or clinging to the object, it is said thus. "They hang down on the earth" (pathaviyā olambanti) means they spread over the surface of the earth. The remaining two words are synonyms and refer to the manner of spreading on the earth. "There, monks, to the fool" (tatra, bhikkhave, bālassa) means, monks, when those objects appear, such a thought arises to the fool.

"He said this" (etadavoca) means a certain monk skilled in connecting the sequence of discourse thought, "The Blessed One did not say it is impossible to give a simile for hell, but only that it is not easy. Although it is not easy, it is possible to do so; let me ask the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) to give a simile for hell," and thus said, "It is possible, Bhante." "They would strike" (haneyyuṃ) means striking in such a way that two blows fall on the same spot by way of piercing through. Because of that piercing, two hundred wounds occur to him. From this point onwards, it should be understood in the same way.

"The size of a hand" (pāṇimattaṃ) means a small stone just large enough to be held in the fist. "Does not even approach the count" (saṅkhampi na upeti) means it does not even reach the measure of counting. "Even a fraction" (kalabhāgampi) means it cannot be said to reach even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-thousandth part. "Even a comparison" (upanidhampi) means it does not even reach the level of being placed nearby for comparison (upanikkhepana); for the observer, there is not even a mere looking. "A red-hot iron stake" (tattaṃ ayokhilaṃ) means after making the three-gāvuta-tall body lie flat on the glowing iron ground, they drive an iron stake the size of a palm tree into his right hand; likewise in the left hand and so forth. Just as they perform this torture (kammakarana) by making him lie on his back, they also do so by making him lie on his chest, right side, and left side. "Having made him lie down" (saṃvesetvā) means making the three-gāvuta-tall body lie on the glowing iron ground. "With axes" (kuṭhārīhi) means the hell-wardens hack him with large axes as big as one side of a house's roof. Blood flows like a river, and flames rising from the iron ground seize the hacked places, causing great suffering.
151:
The hell wardens, like carpenters who mark with a thread, treat the hell-beings as if they were making a wooden pillar with eight or six sides. 'Vāsīhi' refers to adzes the size of a tamarind (referring to the act of carving). With those adzes, the hell wardens slowly carve from the skin down to the bones; every carved place returns to its original state. 'Rathe yojetvā' means yoking them to a chariot blazing on all sides, along with the yoke, ropes, frame, wheels, axle, and goad. 'Mahantaṃ' refers to a mountain of burning embers the size of a large house. 'Āropeṇti' means they make them climb while striking them with blazing iron clubs. Like beans (or rice) placed in a boiling pot, they go up, down, and across as they cook.

'Bhāgaso mito' means divided and set in portions. 'Pariyanto' means surrounded on all sides. 'Ayasā' means covered from above with iron plates.

The light and heat of that fire spread and remain such that the eyes of a person standing and looking from a hundred leagues away would pop out like a pair of marbles.

It means that it is not easy to finish describing hell, even if one speaks for a hundred or a thousand years, saying 'Hell is painful in this way, and painful in that way.'

'Dantullehaṃ' means pulling out with the teeth. 'Rasādo' is one who consumes flavors with greed for taste.

'Aññamaññakhādikā' means devouring one another.

'Dubbaṇṇo' means ugly. 'Duddasiko' means difficult to look at, like an ogre (yakkha) made to frighten children. 'Okoṭimako' means having a stunted body, a neck sunk into the shoulders, and a large belly. 'Kāṇo' means blind in one eye or both eyes. 'Kuṇī' means having one or both hands crooked. 'Pakkhato' means a cripple (pīṭhasappī). The phrase 'he with his body' is begun to show the continuous suffering of that fool.

'Kaliggahēna' means due to losing at dice. 'Adhibandhaṃ nigaccheyya' means that because he has lost so much that all his wealth is insufficient, he even falls into bondage (slavery) himself. 'Kevalā paripūrā bālabhūmi' means the fool fulfills the three types of misconduct and is reborn in hell. Even if he reaches the human world with the remaining results from that hell, he is born into low families, and there too, he fulfills the three types of misconduct and returns to hell. Such a process is called the completion of the fool's sphere.

The characteristics of the wise should be known. Bodily good conduct and so on should be joined with mental good conduct and so on. 'Sīsanhātassa' means the state of one who has bathed including the head (and anointed with perfumes). 'Uposathikassa' means the state of one who has observed the Uposatha.
152:
The fool fulfills misconduct and is reborn in hell. When he comes to the human state due to the remaining results of that kamma, he is born into the five low families, and again fulfilling the three types of misconduct, he is reborn in hell. This process is the complete and full sphere of the fool (bālabhūmi).

The characteristics of the wise and so on should be known in the same manner as previously stated. Here, 'thinking good thoughts' and so on should be applied by way of mental good conduct and so on.

## Explanation of the Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana-vaṇṇanā)

'Sīsaṃ nhātassa' refers to one who has bathed with scented water including the head. 'Uposathikassa' refers to one who possesses the factors of the observed Uposatha. 'Uparipāsādavaragatassa' refers to one who, after ascending to the top of the magnificent palace and eating a good meal, enters the auspicious chamber on the great floor atop the palace and reflects on his virtues (sīla). At that time, it is said, the Wheel-turning Monarch, having given a great gift early in the morning by spending a hundred thousand coins and having again washed his head with sixteen jars of scented water and eaten his breakfast, places his pure upper robe over one shoulder and sits cross-legged on the auspicious couch atop the palace, reflecting on his accumulation of merit consisting in giving. This is the natural custom (dhammatā) of all Wheel-turning Monarchs.

While they are thus reflecting, due to the aforementioned meritorious kamma, the divine Wheel Treasure (dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ) appears, produced by seasonal conditions (utu), resembling a mass of blue sapphires, as if cutting through the surface of the eastern ocean and decorating the sky, endowed with divine power. It is called 'divine' (dibba) because it is joined with divine power. It is called 'thousand-spoked' (sahassāra) because it has a thousand spokes. It is called 'with a rim' (sanemika) because it is with a rim, and 'with a hub' (sanābhika) because it is with a hub. It is called 'complete in every aspect' (sabbākāraparipūra) because it is perfect in all its features.

In that context, it is called 'Wheel Treasure' (cakkaratana) because it is a wheel and also a treasure in the sense of producing delight. The hub, which is called 'with a hub' (sanābhika), is made of sapphire (indanīla). In its center, there is a silver aperture, which shines like a row of pure, smooth teeth as if laughing. Like the moon's disk with a hole in the middle, it is surrounded by silver plates on both outer edges. In the appropriate places of that hub-aperture and the surrounding plates, the dividing lines are well-distributed and clearly visible. This is the perfection of all aspects of the hub of that Wheel Treasure.
153:
Because of those spokes, that Wheel Treasure is called 'Sahassāra' (having a thousand spokes). These spokes are made of the seven gems and are endowed with a radiance like that of the sun's rays. In those spokes, the markings of the divisions and lines are well-defined and clearly visible. This is the perfection of the spokes of the Wheel Treasure in every aspect.

Because of that rim, the Wheel Treasure is called 'Sanemika' (having a rim). That rim is made of very red, pure, and smooth coral (pavāḷa), as if mocking the beauty of the newly risen sun's rays. At the joints of the rim, gold plates of Jambonada gold, possessing the splendor of the evening glow, and the markings of the circular divisions are well-defined and clearly visible. This is the perfection of the rim of the Wheel Treasure in every aspect.

On the outer surface of the rim's circle, between every ten spokes, there is a coral rod (pavāḷadaṇḍa) that is hollow inside like a flute, decorated with circular holes, and capable of catching the wind. When struck by the wind, it produces a sound like a five-fold musical ensemble (pañcaṅgika-tūriya) played by a highly skilled musician—a sound that is melodious, enchanting, and delightful. Above that coral rod is a white parasol (setacchatta), and on both sides are rows of hanging flower garlands. Thus, surrounded by two hundred rows of hanging flower garlands, and adorned with a hundred coral rods bearing a hundred white parasols, the rim's circumference is exceedingly beautiful. Inside the two openings of the hub, there are two lion-mouths (sīhamukha). From these, two pearl strings (muttakalāpa) hang down, as large as palm trunks, possessing the splendor of the full moon's rays, and ending in red woolen balls resembling the newly risen sun, as if surpassing the beauty of the celestial Ganges' flow. When these pearl strings revolve in the sky along with the Wheel Treasure, they appear as if three wheels are revolving together. This is its perfection in every way and in every aspect.

The Wheel Treasure, thus perfect in every aspect, usually approaches the royal capital after people have eaten their evening meal, while they are sitting on seats prepared at their doors engaged in conversation, and while children are playing at crossroads and such places. It beautifies the sky at a height that is neither too high nor too low, near the tops of the forest groves, as if adorning the tips of the tree branches. It causes the ears of beings to listen with its sweet sound heard from twelve yojanas away, and it draws the eyes of beings with its color, brilliant with the gathering of various radiances, from one yojana away...
154:
...approaching the royal capital as if proclaiming the power of the Universal Monarch's merit. Then, upon merely hearing the sound of that Wheel Treasure, those people, their hearts pondering, 'From where does this sound come? Whose sound is this?' look toward the east. One of them says, 'Friends, how wonderful! Previously, this full moon rose alone, but today it has risen as a pair. Like a pair of royal swans (hamsa), this pair of full moons is soaring through the sky one after the other.' Another says, 'Friend, what are you saying? Where and when have you ever seen two full moons rising together? Indeed, this is the rising sun, possessing heat-producing radiance and rays spread out like a peacock's tail.' Another, smiling, says, 'Are you mad? Has the sun not just set? How could that sun rise again, following this full moon? Surely, this must be the celestial mansion (vimāna) of a meritorious person, brilliant with the radiance of many gems.'

While all those people were thus disparaging each other and speaking, the Wheel Treasure left the path of the moon and headed toward the King's palace. Then, when they asked, 'For whose benefit has this appeared?' others replied, 'For no one else; is our King not one who has fulfilled the duties of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti-vatta)? It has appeared for that King.' Then, all the people who were speaking and all who saw it followed after the Wheel Treasure. That Wheel Treasure, as if wishing to make known its arrival for the King's sake, circled the city seven times from above the city walls, circumambulated the King's palace clockwise (padakkhiṇa), and then came to rest near the northern lion-window (sīhapañjara) of the palace, at a place where it could easily be honored with perfumes and flowers, standing as if fixed on an axle.

When the Wheel Treasure stood thus, the King, seeing the mass of radiance shining within the palace with the light of various multi-colored gems entering through the windows and other openings, felt a strong desire to see it. His attendants also came with the gift of pleasant words and reported the matter. Then the King, his body suffused with intense joy and rapture, rose from his seat and went near the lion-window. Seeing the Wheel Treasure and wishing to perform the ritual as known from the Buddha's teaching, he rose from his seat, lifted a golden pitcher with his left hand, held it with his right, and poured water, saying, 'May the noble Wheel Treasure roll forth; may the noble Wheel Treasure be victorious.' At that moment, the Universal Monarch became endowed with the seven treasures.
155:
Releasing his cross-legged posture, he rose from his seat and went near the lion-window. Upon seeing that Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana), he thought, "I have heard this before," and so on. Therefore, it is said: "The Khattiya King, having seen... Am I indeed a Wheel-turning Monarch?" In that passage, "that King is a Wheel-turning Monarch"—by what measure does one become a Wheel-turning Monarch? When the Wheel Treasure rises into the sky to the height of one or two finger-breadths and revolves, he becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch.

Now, to show the ritual to be performed to set that Wheel Treasure in motion, the Buddha said: "Then, O monks," and so on. In that passage, "rising from his seat" means getting up from where he was sitting and coming near the Wheel Treasure. "Taking a pitcher" means lifting a golden pitcher (bhiṅkāra) with a spout like an elephant's trunk with the left hand and taking the water with the right hand. Saying, "May the noble Wheel Treasure revolve; may the noble Wheel Treasure be victorious," he pours the ceremonial water. In the passage "The Wheel-turning Monarch follows with his fourfold army," for all Wheel-turning Monarchs, immediately after pouring the water and saying "May the noble Wheel Treasure be victorious," the Wheel Treasure rises into the air and revolves. At the very moment it revolves, that King receives the title of Wheel-turning Monarch.

When the Wheel Treasure revolves, the Wheel-turning Monarch, following that Wheel Treasure, mounts his noble vehicle and rises into the sky. Then, the retinue carrying the parasol, fly-whisks, and so on, as well as the members of the inner palace, surround him. Thereafter, the Crown Prince, the General, and others, along with their respective armies adorned with various tunics and armor, brilliant with the light of various weapons, and decorated with hoisted banners and flags, also rise into the sky and surround the Wheel-turning Monarch.

The King's ministers, to honor the people, have drums beaten in the city streets, saying, "Friends, the Wheel Treasure has appeared to our Great King. Assemble yourselves, adorned and prepared according to your own wealth." The multitude, naturally drawn by the sound of the Wheel Treasure alone, abandon all their tasks, take perfumes, flowers, and so on, and assemble. All those people also rise into the sky and surround the Wheel-turning Monarch. Whoever develops the desire to go with the King reaches the sky. Thus, there is an assembly twelve yojanas in length and breadth. In that assembly, there is not a single person with a deformed body or soiled clothes. For the Wheel-turning Monarch has a pure retinue. The assembly of a Wheel-turning Monarch, like an assembly of Vidyādharas, while traveling in the sky...
156:
...resembles jewels scattered upon a slab of Indanīla (sapphire). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The Wheel-turning Monarch follows only behind (the Wheel Treasure) with his fourfold army."

That Wheel Treasure also travels, revolving in the sky not too high above the treetops. Those who desire the flowers, fruits, and shoots of the trees can easily take them. Those on the ground can distinguish: "This is the King, this is the Crown Prince, this is the General." Among the postures such as standing, whoever wishes to travel in a certain posture travels in that very posture. Those devoted to arts such as painting travel while performing their respective tasks within this multitude. Just as on the ground, all their tasks are accomplished in the sky. Thus, taking the assembly of the Wheel-turning Monarch, that Wheel Treasure, leaving Mount Sineru on the left, travels over the ocean to Pubbavideha, which measures eight thousand yojanas.

In that island, in a delightful region with a pure and level ground, well-shaded and watered, where food and supplies are easily obtained, and which is suitable for the settlement of an assembly twelve yojanas in diameter and thirty-six yojanas in circumference, that Wheel Treasure stands in the sky as if fixed by an axle. Then, by that sign, the multitude descends to the ground and dwells there, performing all their tasks such as bathing and eating as they please. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, in whatever region that Wheel Treasure stays, there the Wheel-turning Monarch dwells with his fourfold army."

When the Wheel-turning Monarch thus dwells there, the kings of that region, even upon hearing that "the enemy's power has arrived," do not assemble their forces to prepare for war. Immediately upon the appearance of the Wheel Treasure, there is no being who dares to lift a weapon against the King with the thought of being an enemy. This is the power of the Wheel Treasure.

By the power of the Wheel,
All the enemies of that King come to be subdued.
Because he subdues enemies, for that Lord of Men,
That treasure is called his Cakka (Wheel/Command).
157:
Therefore, all those kings, bringing gifts in accordance with their own royal glory and wealth, approached that Wheel-turning Monarch. With bowed heads, they worshipped his feet with the consecration of the radiance of the gems at the tips of their crowns, and with words such as "Come, Great King," they submitted to his service. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, in the East... Great King, please give us instruction."

In that passage, "svāgataṃ" means a good arrival. For when some people arrive, others grieve, and when they depart, others rejoice. When some people arrive, others rejoice, and when they depart, others grieve. You, Great King, are of such a nature that your arrival brings joy and your departure brings sorrow. Therefore, it is said that your arrival is a good arrival. When this was said by the kings, the Wheel-turning Monarch did not say, "Pay me this much annual tax," nor did he seize the wealth of one king to give to another. Instead, with wisdom befitting his status as a Righteous King (Dhamma-Rāja), he examined the faults of killing and so forth. With a lovely and pleasant voice, he taught the Dhamma in this manner: "Look, dear ones, killing (pāṇātipāta), when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads to hell." He gave such advice as: "One should not kill living beings." Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The Wheel-turning Monarch spoke thus: 'One should not kill living beings... and enjoy your possessions as you have formerly done.'"

Do all kings accept this advice of the Monarch? Even the advice of the Buddha is not yet accepted by everyone; why then would they all accept the advice of the Monarch? Therefore, only those who are wise and discerning accept it. However, all kings follow the lead of the Wheel-turning Monarch. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the words: "Monks, those who..."

Thereafter, when the Wheel-treasure had thus given advice to the inhabitants of the Eastern Continent (Pubbavideha), and after the morning meal was finished, it rose into the sky together with the army of the Wheel-turning Monarch and entered the Eastern Ocean. As it entered, the waters of the great ocean receded by the measure of one league (yojana), standing like a wall of beryl (veḷuriya) within the sea, just as a cobra king lowers its hood upon smelling an antidote, thus calming the expansion of the waves. At that very moment, as if wishing to see the glory of the King's merit, various jewels scattered at the bottom of the great ocean came from here and there and filled that area of one league. Then, the King's retinue, seeing the bottom of the great ocean filled with various jewels, took them as they pleased in the folds of their garments and so forth; as they pleased...
158:
When the retinue had taken the jewels as they pleased, the Wheel-treasure withdrew and returned. As it returned, the retinue went in front, the King in the middle, and the Wheel-treasure at the very rear. The ocean water also followed closely without any gap, rising up to the rim of the wheel's circumference, as if enticed by the glory of the Wheel-treasure or as if unable to bear separation from it.

In this way, the Wheel-turning Monarch, having conquered the Eastern Continent (Pubbavideha) bounded by the Eastern Ocean, and desiring to conquer the Southern Continent (Jambudīpa) bounded by the Southern Ocean, proceeded toward the Southern Ocean by the path shown by the Wheel-treasure. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Then, monks, that Wheel-treasure, having entered the Eastern Ocean and emerged from it, turned toward the South." The manner of its turning, the mobilization of the army, the arrival of the opposing kings, the giving of advice to them, the entering into the Southern Ocean, the receding of the ocean waters, and the taking of jewels—all should be understood in the same manner as previously described.

Having conquered that Jambudīpa, which is ten thousand leagues in extent, and having emerged from the Southern Ocean, he proceeded in the same manner as previously described to conquer the Western Continent (Aparagoyāna), which is seven thousand leagues in extent. Having conquered that continent up to the edge of the ocean in the same way, and having emerged from the Western Ocean, he proceeded in the same manner to conquer the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), which is eight thousand leagues in extent. Having conquered that continent up to the edge of the ocean in the same way, he emerged from the Northern Ocean.

By this extent, the Wheel-turning Monarch attained sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans. Having thus achieved victory, in order to view the perfection of his royal glory, he rose into the upper sky with his retinue and looked upon the four great continents, each surrounded by five hundred small islands, as if looking upon four lakes adorned with well-bloomed red, blue, and white lotuses. He then returned to his own royal capital in due order by the path shown by the Wheel-treasure. Then, the Wheel-treasure stood as if beautifying the gate of the inner palace.

When the Wheel-treasure is thus established in the royal palace, there is no need for torches, lamps, or lanterns. The radiance of the Wheel-treasure alone dispels the darkness of the night. However, for those who desire darkness during the night, there is indeed darkness. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Having entered the Southern Ocean... such a Wheel-treasure appears."
159:
## Description of the Elephant Treasure

When the Wheel Treasure had thus appeared, the ministers of that Wheel-turning Monarch had a clean portion of ground prepared at the site of the ordinary auspicious elephant, and had it smeared with fragrant perfumes such as red and white sandalwood. They scattered fragrant flowers of various colors on the ground below, and above, they prepared a canopy decorated with delightful garlands of flowers interspersed with golden stars, making it like a celestial mansion. Then they addressed the King, saying, "O King, please reflect upon the arrival of such an Elephant Treasure."

The Wheel-turning Monarch, having given great alms in the manner previously described and having undertaken the precepts, sat reflecting on the perfection of that merit. Then, urged by the power of the King's merit, an excellent elephant—desiring to enjoy such special honor—arrived at that place from either the Chaddanta lineage or the Uposatha lineage. It had a pure white body, with feet, neck, eyes, and mouth as red as the rising sun. It stood firmly on seven points, with well-proportioned limbs and a trunk as beautiful as a blooming red lotus. Possessing psychic power and able to travel through the sky like a yogi, it was like a kingly silver mountain with edges tinged with the powder of red arsenic (manosilā).

If it comes from the Chaddanta lineage, the youngest elephant comes; if from the Uposatha lineage, the eldest comes. In the Pali text, however, it is mentioned only as "the elephant king named Uposatha." This elephant king comes only to those Wheel-turning Monarchs who have fulfilled the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch and reflect as described in the Cakkavatti Sutta; it does not come to others. It comes of its own accord to the site of the ordinary auspicious elephant, displaces the existing auspicious elephant, and stands in its place. Therefore, the Blessed One taught, "Bhikkhus, once more... the elephant king..." and so forth.

Seeing the Elephant Treasure that had thus appeared, the elephant keepers and others, filled with joy, went quickly and informed the King. The Wheel-turning Monarch came in great haste and, seeing the Elephant Treasure with a clear and trusting mind, thought, "Friends, the elephant vehicle is indeed excellent, if only it would submit to training," and he stretched out his hand. Then, the elephant king, wishing to show its docility like a domestic calf, lowered its ears and approached the King. The King desired to mount the elephant. Seeing the King's wish, his attendants decorated the Elephant Treasure with golden banners and golden ornaments, covered it with a golden net, and brought it before the King.

The King, without making the elephant kneel, mounted it by a ladder made of the seven gems, with his mind intent on traveling through the sky. Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, the elephant king soared into the sky, which was as dark blue as the radiance of an emerald (indanilā), like a king of swans. Then, as described in the movement of the Wheel Treasure, the entire royal retinue followed. Thus, the Wheel-turning Monarch, together with his retinue, traveled over the entire earth and returned to the capital before breakfast. Such is the great power of the Wheel-turning Monarch's Elephant Treasure. Therefore, the Blessed One taught, "Such an Elephant Treasure appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch."

Now, the Horse Treasure will be described. When the Elephant Treasure had thus appeared, the attendants of the Wheel-turning Monarch had the site of the ordinary auspicious horse prepared with a clean and level ground, decorated it, and urged the King to reflect on the arrival of the Horse Treasure in the same manner as before. The Wheel-turning Monarch, having performed alms-giving and undertaken the precepts as before, sat on the upper level of the palace, repeatedly reflecting on the perfection of his merit. Then, urged by the power of the King's merit, from the Sindhava (Sindhu) breed, a horse appeared with a body as radiant as a cluster of white clouds in the autumn sky, entwined with streaks of lightning.
160:
In the same manner as described for the movement of the Wheel Treasure, the entire royal retinue followed. Thus, the Wheel-turning Monarch, together with his retinue, traveled over the entire earth and returned to the capital before breakfast. Such is the great power of the Wheel-turning Monarch's Elephant Treasure. Therefore, the Blessed One taught, "...to the Wheel-turning Monarch... such an Elephant Treasure appears."

## Description of the Horse Treasure

When the Elephant Treasure had thus appeared, the ministers and attendants of the Wheel-turning Monarch prepared and decorated the site of the ordinary auspicious horse to be clean and level, and they exerted effort to bring about the arrival of that Horse Treasure in the same manner as before. The Wheel-turning Monarch also performed alms-giving and undertook the precepts as before, and while sitting on the palace terrace, he repeatedly reflected on the perfection of his own merit. Then, urged by the power of the Wheel-turning Monarch's merit, from the Sindhava breed, the horse king named Valāhaka arrived and stood at that place. It had a body as radiant as a cluster of white clouds in the autumn sky, entwined with streaks of lightning; it had red feet and a red muzzle. Its body was pure, smooth, and solid like a mass of moonlight. Because it had a head as black as a crow's neck or an emerald (indanilā), it was called 'Kāḷasīsa' (Black-head). Because it possessed a mane that was fine, rounded, and straight like Muñja grass, as if it had been well-groomed, it was called 'Muñjakesa' (Muñja-hair). It was capable of traveling through the sky. All other details should be understood in the same way as described for the Elephant Treasure. Referring to such a Horse Treasure, the Blessed One taught the words beginning with "Puna caparaṃ" (Once more).

## Description of the Gem Treasure

When the Horse Treasure had thus appeared to the Wheel-turning Monarch, the Gem Treasure arrived from Mount Vepulla. It was four cubits in length and had the size of a cart's hub. It was decorated at both ends with two golden lotuses and clusters of very pure pearls hanging from the edges. It was surrounded by eighty-four thousand jewels and diffused a splendor like that of the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. When the Gem Treasure arrived, it was placed in a net of pearls and raised on a series of bamboo poles to a height of about sixty cubits in the sky. During the night, its radiance spread over an area of about one league (yojana) all around. Because of that radiance, the entire area became illuminated as if it were the time of dawn. Then, farmers began their farming work, and merchants...
161:
Shops are opened. Various craftsmen perform their respective tasks, thinking it is daytime. Therefore, [the Buddha] said: "Monks, furthermore... the Gem-treasure appears."

## Description of the Queen-treasure (Itthiratanā)
For the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) for whom the Gem-treasure has thus appeared, the Queen-treasure appears as a cause for special sensual pleasure. They bring his Chief Queen from the Madda royal family, or she comes of her own accord from Uttarakuru due to the power of [the King's] merit. Her other accomplishments are mentioned in the Pāḷi text itself: "Monks, furthermore, for the Wheel-turning Monarch, the Queen-treasure appears, beautiful, lovely to behold," and so forth.

In that Pāḷi text, she is called 'Abhirūpā' (beautiful) because of her superior appearance due to the perfection of her physical form. She delights the eyes of those who look at her; therefore, she is called 'Dassanīyā' (lovely to behold) because she is worthy of being looked at even by abandoning other tasks. She gladdens the mind with joy for the one who looks at her; therefore, she is called 'Pāsādikā' (inspiring confidence). 'Paramāya' means supreme because she brings such clarity. 'Vaṇṇapokkharatāya' means beauty of complexion, and 'Samannāgatā' means endowed with.

Alternatively, she is 'Abhirūpā' because she is neither too tall nor too short. She is 'Dassanīyā' because she is neither too thin nor too fat. She is 'Pāsādikā' because she is neither too dark nor too fair. She is 'endowed with supreme beauty of complexion' because she has surpassed the human complexion but has not yet reached the divine complexion. Indeed, the radiance of humans does not emanate outward, while the radiance of devas emanates very far. However, the radiance of the Queen-treasure's body illuminates an area of about twelve cubits.

Among the terms "not too tall" etc., the first pair describes the perfection of height, the second pair describes the perfection of girth, and the third pair describes the perfection of complexion. Or, these six terms describe the absence of physical defects, while the phrase "surpassing the human complexion" describes physical perfection.

Her bodily touch is like that of silk-cotton or cotton-wool that has been carded a hundred times and dipped in the cream of ghee. 'Sīte' means [she is warm] when the King is cold. 'Uṇhe' means [she is cool] when the King is hot. 'Candanagandho' means the scent of fresh sandalwood, well-ground and mixed with the four types of fragrances, wafts from her body at all times. 'Uppalagandho' means the scent, extremely fragrant like a blue lotus just blossomed at that moment, wafts from her mouth when she laughs or speaks.
162:
Thus, to show the conduct appropriate to the physical perfection of the Queen-treasure, who is endowed with the perfection of touch and scent, the words beginning with "Taṃ kho pana" were spoken. In those words, she is called 'Pubbuṭṭhāyinī' (rising before) because, upon seeing the Wheel-turning Monarch, she rises first from her seat without delay, like one being burned by fire. She is called 'Pacchānipātinī' (lying down after) because she performs tasks such as fanning the King with a palm-leaf fan when he is seated, and only afterwards does she sleep or sit. She is called 'Kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī' (obeying commands) because she heeds the King's orders, asking, "What shall I do, O King?" She is called 'Manāpacārinī' (acting pleasingly) because she acts only in ways that please the King. She is called 'Piyavādinī' (speaking endearingly) because she speaks only words that are dear and beloved to the King.

Now, to show that the conduct of the Queen-treasure is due only to the purity of her intention and not due to deceit, the words beginning with "Taṃ kho pana" were spoken. Therein, "No aticarati" means she does not transgress; it means she does not desire another man even in her mind. The qualities mentioned at the beginning of the description of the Queen-treasure, such as 'Abhirūpā', and those at the end, such as 'Pubbuṭṭhāyinī', are her natural qualities. However, the qualities such as "surpassing the human complexion" should be understood as arising from the power of previous merit, starting from the appearance of the Wheel-treasure (Cakkaratanā), depending on the merit of the Wheel-turning Monarch. Alternatively, even the qualities such as beauty became perfect in every aspect starting from the appearance of the Wheel-treasure. Therefore, it is said: "Such a Queen-treasure appears."

## Description of the Householder-treasure (Gahapatiratanā)
For the Wheel-turning Monarch who has the Queen-treasure thus appeared, the Householder-treasure appears so that tasks involving wealth may be accomplished as desired. That householder is naturally very wealthy, born into a wealthy family, and is a treasurer who increases the King's mass of wealth. Along with the power of the Wheel-treasure, a divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) produced by the result of his kamma appears to that householder, with which he sees treasures within a distance of one yojana inside the earth. Seeing that abundance, he goes to the King with a joyful heart, invites him to use the wealth, and accomplishes all tasks that must be done with wealth. Therefore, it is said: "Monks, furthermore... such a Householder-treasure appears."

## Description of the Counselor-treasure (Pariṇāyakaratanā)
For the Wheel-turning Monarch who has the Householder-treasure thus appeared, the Counselor-treasure appears, who is capable of managing all affairs. That Treasure-son is indeed the King's eldest son.
163:
(The Counselor Treasure) is naturally wise, clever, and possessed of sagacity that penetrates causes. However, by relying on the power of the Great King’s merit and through the power of his own karma, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa) arises in him. With that knowledge of others' minds, he is able to know the thoughts and intentions of the royal retinue within twelve yojanas, and is capable of advising the Great King on what is detrimental and what is beneficial. That Counselor Treasure, seeing his own capability, becomes joyful and invites the Great King to allow him to manage and advise on all matters. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Furthermore... the Counselor Treasure (pariṇāyakaratanā) appears." In that passage, "ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetုံ" means to appoint the ministers who should be appointed to their respective positions.

The terms beginning with "samavepākiniyā" have already been explained below.

"Kaṭaggahēna" means by obtaining victory. "Mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ" refers to a great mass of wealth worth two or three hundred thousand in a single stroke. "Kevalā paripūrā paṇḍitabhūmi" means that a wise person, having fulfilled the three types of good conduct, is reborn in the celestial realm; when returning from there to the human world, he is reborn endowed with noble lineage, beauty, and great wealth; while remaining in that human life, he again fulfills the three types of good conduct and is reborn once more in the celestial realm. This state of complete perfection is the "ground of the wise" (paṇḍitabhūmi). All the remaining terms are clear and easy to understand.
