## 10. Devadūta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Devadūta Sutta. In that sutta, the terms beginning with "dve agārā" have already been explained in detail in the Assapura Sutta.

Regarding the phrase "nirayaṃ upapannā," the Blessed One, in some teachings, begins with hell and concludes with the celestial realm; in other teachings, He begins with the celestial realm and concludes with hell. If He wishes to explain the bliss of the celestial realm in detail, He speaks of the suffering of hell only in part. He also speaks of the suffering of the animal realm, the suffering of the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), and the bliss of the human world only in part, while explaining the bliss of the celestial realm in detail. If He wishes to explain the suffering of hell in detail...
164: The Blessed One speaks of the bliss and prosperity in the celestial and human worlds, as well as the suffering in the animal and hungry ghost realms, only in part, while elaborating extensively on the suffering in hell. In this sutta, because He wishes to explain the suffering of hell in detail, He begins the teaching from the celestial realm and concludes it with hell. Having spoken briefly of the prosperity of gods and humans and the suffering of animals and hungry ghosts, He said, "Monks, the hell-wardens..." and so forth, in order to explain the suffering of hell in detail. In this regard, some elders of the Vijnanavada school say, "There are no such things as hell-wardens; it is only karma that inflicts torture like a machine." Their view is refuted in the Abhidhamma (Kathāvatthu) by such methods as: "Are there hell-wardens in hell? Yes, there are; and there are also those who inflict torture." Just as there are executioners who carry out punishments in the human world, so too there are truly hell-wardens in hell. In the phrase "of King Yama," King Yama is a king of the mansion-dwelling ghosts (vemānika-peta). At one time, he enjoys prosperity such as celestial mansions, celestial wishing-trees, celestial gardens, and celestial dancers; at another time, he experiences the results of his karma. He is a righteous king. Moreover, he is not alone; there are four such kings at the four gates. When asking, "Have you not seen?", it is said with reference to the absence of any divine messenger (devadūta) sent to him. Then King Yama, realizing "This person does not grasp the meaning of what is said," and wishing to make him understand, says, "My good man..." and so forth. "Jātidhammo" means having the nature of birth, not being free from birth, meaning "Birth exists within me." The same method should be understood for subsequent terms like "jarādhammo" (subject to old age). In the context of "having examined the first divine messenger," a very young infant, in terms of meaning, is said to speak thus: "Friends, look, I have hands and feet just like yours. However, I am wallowing in my own excrement and urine, unable to get up and bathe of my own accord. I have a soiled body and cannot even speak to ask someone to bathe me. I have become like this because I am not yet free from birth. Not only I, but you too are not free from birth. Just as birth has come to me, so too birth will come to you. Therefore, perform meritorious deeds before that birth arrives." For this reason, that infant is called a divine messenger (devadūta). The etymological meaning is as stated in the Maghadeva Sutta.
165:
Regarding the second divine messenger (devadūta), an extremely aged being essentially says: "O friends, look at me. I too was once young like you, endowed with the strength of thighs, the strength of arms, and speed. Those strengths and speeds of mine have disappeared. Although I have hands and feet, they no longer perform their functions. I have come to such a state because I am not yet liberated from old age. It is not that I alone am not liberated from old age; you too are not yet liberated from old age. Just as old age has come to me, so too will old age come to you. Therefore, perform wholesome deeds even before that old age arrives." For this reason, such a person is called a divine messenger.

Regarding the third divine messenger, a sick being essentially says: "O friends, look at me. I too was once free from disease like you. Now, I am oppressed by illness, wallowing in my own excrement and urine, unable even to rise. Although I have hands and feet, they no longer perform their functions. I have come to such a state because I am not yet liberated from disease. It is not that I alone am not liberated from disease; you too are not yet liberated from disease. Just as disease has come to me, so too will disease come to you. Therefore, perform wholesome deeds even before that disease arrives." For this reason, such a person is called a divine messenger.

Regarding the fourth divine messenger, either the punishments (kammakaraṇa) or the executioners (kammakaraṇika) should be understood as divine messengers. In the case of punishments, the thirty-two types of punishment essentially say: "When we arise, we do not arise on trees or stones; we arise only on the bodies of those like you. Therefore, perform wholesome deeds even before we arise." For this reason, those punishments are called divine messengers. The executioners also essentially say: "When we perform the thirty-two types of punishment, we do not perform them on trees and such; we perform them only on beings like you. Therefore, perform wholesome deeds even before we perform punishments on you." For this reason, they too are called divine messengers.

Regarding the fifth divine messenger, a deceased being essentially says: "O friends, look at me, cast away in a cemetery for corpses, having reached a state such as being bloated. I have come to such a state because I am not yet liberated from death. It is not only I..."
166:
...you too are not yet liberated from death. Just as death has come to me, so too will death come to you. Therefore, perform wholesome deeds even before that death arrives." (It is as if the deceased says this essentially.) For this reason, this deceased person is also called a divine messenger (devadūta).

As to who receives this interrogation by the divine messengers and who does not: one who has committed many evil deeds simply goes directly to hell. Only one who has committed a small amount of evil deeds receives this interrogation. This should be understood through the following analogy: just as a thief caught with stolen goods is not interrogated but is given the appropriate punishment immediately, whereas a person caught after investigation is taken to the place of judgment and receives an interrogation. Those with few evil deeds may remember their merits by their own nature, or they may remember when reminded by King Yama.

Among them, the one named Dīghajayanta the Damila remembered by his own nature. It is said that this Damila had once offered a red cloth to the Ākāsacetiya at Sumanagiri Vihāra. Later, when he was reborn near the Ussada hell, upon hearing the sound of the flames of hell, he remembered the cloth he had offered and was reborn in heaven. Another person, while giving a robe that had been worn to his son, a young monk, placed it at his feet. At the time of death, he took as a sign (nimitta) the "pata-pata" sound [of the cloth]. While he was reborn near the Ussada hell, because of the sound of the flames, he remembered that robe and was reborn in heaven. In this way, they first remember their wholesome deeds by their own nature and are reborn in heaven.

For those who cannot remember by their own nature, [Yama] asks about the five divine messengers. Then, some remember through the first divine messenger, and some through the second and so on. For one who does not remember even through all five, King Yama himself reminds him. It is said that a certain minister, having offered a pot of jasmine flowers to the Mahācetiya, shared the merit with Yama. Due to unwholesome karma, he was reborn in hell and brought before Yama. When he did not remember his merit even when questioned about the five divine messengers, Yama himself, looking and reflecting, saw it and reminded him: "Did you not offer a pot of jasmine flowers to the Mahācetiya and share the merit with me?" At that time, he remembered and went to the celestial realm. If Yama himself looks and does not see anything, he remains silent, thinking, "This being will surely experience great suffering."

"Mahāniraya" refers to the Avīci Great Hell. As for its dimensions: the interior length and breadth are each one hundred yojanas. It has an iron floor and an iron roof, and each wall is nine yojanas thick. To the east...
167:
The flame from the wall rises, takes hold of the back wall, pierces through that wall, and extends a hundred yojanas beyond. In the other directions, it is the same. Thus, by the extent of the flames, the length and breadth are three hundred and eighteen yojanas. In circumference, it is nine hundred and fifty-four yojanas. All around, including the Ussada hells, it is ten thousand yojanas.

Regarding the phrase "ubbhataṃ tādisameva hoti," the foot that treads is so firmly planted down to the bone that it cannot even be lifted. The meaning here is: it burns starting from the lower part, and it burns starting from the upper part; thus, it is evident that it burns at the time of treading, and it remains exactly the same at the time of lifting. Therefore, it is said so. "Bahu-sampatto" means reaching many hundreds and thousands of years.

Why is this hell known by the name 'Avīci'? 'Vīci' means an interval or gap. In that hell, there is no interval between the flames, the beings, or the suffering. Therefore, that hell is known by the name Avīci. Indeed, the flame from its eastern wall rises and, being continuous, goes for a hundred yojanas, pierces the western wall, and extends a hundred yojanas beyond. In the other directions, it is the same.

Devadatta is born in the midst of these six flames. His body is a hundred yojanas in size. Both feet are submerged into the iron ground up to the ankles. Both hands are submerged into the iron walls up to the wrists. The head is submerged into the iron roof up to the brow bone. From the lower part, an iron stake pierces the body and is fixed into the roof. A stake coming from the eastern wall pierces the heart and enters the western wall. A stake coming from the northern wall pierces the ribs and enters the southern wall. Because of his offense against the unshakable Tathāgata, he must be cooked while remaining unshakable (motionless). He has reached such a state because it is similar to the kamma he committed. Thus, because there is no interval between the flames, it is called Avīci.

Furthermore, within that space of a hundred yojanas, beings are packed without interval, like flour pounded and filled into a tube. It cannot be said, "There is a being in this place, but not in that place." There is no interval between those who are going, standing, sitting, or lying down. Whether going, standing, sitting, or lying down, they do not obstruct one another. Thus, because there is no interval between beings, it is called Avīci.
168:
In the body-door, six types of consciousness accompanied by equanimity arise, and one type of consciousness accompanied by pain arises. Even so, just as when six drops of honey are placed on the tip of the tongue and one drop of hot liquid copper is placed there, only the hot copper drop is evident due to the intensity of the burning, while the other honey drops are negligible (not reckoned); similarly, due to the intensity of the burning of the hellfire, only the painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is evident without interval in this Avīci hell. The other moments of consciousness accompanied by equanimity are not reckoned. Thus, because there is no interval in suffering, it is called Avīci.

"Mahanto" means it is a hundred yojanas in size. "So tattha patati" means one foot of that person is in the Great Hell, and one foot falls into the Excrement Hell (Gūtha-niraya). "Sūcimukhā" refers to worms with needle-like mouths. These needle-mouthed worms are the size of an elephant's neck in circumference, or the size of a single-log boat in length.

"Kukkula-nirayo" is the Hot Ash Hell, a hundred yojanas in size, filled with glowing embers without flames, like the interior of a peaked house. Beings who fall into that hell sink right to the bottom, like wax-fruits or similar objects thrown into a heap of hot ashes.

"Āropenti" means the hell-wardens strike them with iron clubs and make them climb. When those denizens of hell climb, the thorns point downwards; when they descend, the thorns point upwards.

"Vāteritāni" means they are moved by winds born of kamma. "Hatthampi chindanti" means they cut them as if mincing meat on a board. If they get up and flee, an iron wall rises and surrounds them, and from below, razor-edges appear.

"Khārodakā nadī" is the river of caustic water named Vetaraṇī, which is a river of molten copper. In that river, there are coarse sand-plains made of iron and iron lotus leaves as sharp as razors. Below, there are razor-edges, and on both banks, there are rattan canes and kusa grass. That denizen of hell, while being drifted up and down in that river, is cut by the lotus leaves, pierced by the thorns on the crossroad-shaped coarse sand-plains, sliced by the razor-edges, scratched by the kusa grass on both banks, dragged by the rattan canes, and split by sharp spears.
169:
"With a hot iron hook" means that when the hell-being says, "I am very hungry," they fill a large iron basket with iron balls and approach him. Knowing they are iron balls, he clenches his teeth. Then the hell-wardens open his mouth with a hot iron hook. They bring molten copper in a large iron pot and do the same. "Again in the Great Hell" means that starting from the fivefold binding up to the drinking of molten copper, and from the drinking of molten copper back to the fivefold binding and so on, they perform these and then cast him back into the Great Hell. Among those hell-beings, some are released at the fivefold binding itself, some at the second stage, some at the third, and some when drinking the molten copper. However, if the unwholesome kamma is not yet exhausted, they are cast back into the Great Hell.

A young monk learning this Devadūta Sutta asked, "Venerable Sir, is a being who has experienced such suffering cast back into the Great Hell again?" The teacher replied, "Yes, friend, as long as the unwholesome kamma is not exhausted, they do this repeatedly." The monk said, "Venerable Sir, let the recitation (uddesa) wait; please teach me only the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)." Having been taught the meditation subject, he became a Sotāpanna and then returned to take up the recitation. The number of other monks in this region who set aside the recitation and attained Arahatship is beyond counting. All Buddhas never abandon this Devadūta Sutta and always preach it.

"Hīnakāyūpagā" means having approached a low group. "Upādāne" refers to clinging through craving and views. "Jātimaraṇasambhava" refers to [the clinging] which is the cause of birth and death. "Anupādā" means without clinging through the four types of clinging. "Jātimaraṇasaṅkhaye" means they are liberated in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of birth and death.

"Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā" means they are cooled by the extinction of all defilements in this very existence. "Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccaguṃ" means they are said to have transcended all suffering.

170:
## 4. Vibhaṅga Vagga
## 1. Bhaddekaratta Sutta Vaṇṇanā
The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Bhaddekaratta Sutta. In that Bhaddekaratta Sutta, "bhaddekarattassa" refers to a person who has an auspicious night because of being endowed with the practice of insight (vipassanā). "Uddesa" refers to the summary (mātikā). "Vibhaṅga" refers to the teaching that is the detailed analysis.

"Atītaṃ" refers to the past five aggregates. "Nānvāgameyya" means one should not follow after them with craving and views. "Nappaṭikaṅkhe" means one should not long for them with craving and views. The phrase "Yadatītaṃ" etc., is the statement of reason here. Because the past five aggregates have been abandoned, have ceased, and have reached destruction, one should not follow after those five aggregates again with craving and views. Because the future five aggregates have not yet been reached, have not yet arisen, and have not yet been produced, one should not long for those future five aggregates either.

"Tattha tattha" means that in whatever moment the present five aggregates arise, in that very moment, a person observes those present five aggregates with the seven types of insight, such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), or he practices insight in various places such as forests. "Asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ" (unshakeable, unagitated) is spoken to show insight (vipassanā) and the reviewing of insight (paṭivipassanā). Because insight is not pulled back or destroyed by lust and so on, it is called "asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ"; the meaning is that one should develop that insight and review it again. Alternatively, Nibbāna is called "asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ" because it is not pulled back or destroyed by lust and so on. The wise monk should develop that Nibbāna; the meaning is that he should develop it by repeatedly taking it as an object and attaining the respective fruit-attainments (phalasamāpatti).

For the benefit of one who so develops: "Ajjeva kiccamātappaṃ" means that the effort (vīriya) which has received the name "ātappa" because it burns and scorches the defilements should be made this very day. "Ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve" means who can know whether there will be life or death tomorrow? It shows that one should make effort in this way: "I will give dana, or keep the precepts, or perform some other merit this very day," without letting the thought arise, "There is still delay (papañca) today; I will do it tomorrow or the day after." "Mahāsenena" means the many causes of death such as fire, poison, and weapons are the army of that King of Death; with such a King of Death who has a great army, there is no bargaining (saṅgara) in the form of making friends, saying, "Wait for three or eight days until I perform my own refuge-work such as worshipping the Buddha"; nor is there bargaining in the form of giving a bribe, saying, "Take this hundred or thousand and wait for three or eight days"; nor is there bargaining in the form of gathering troops, saying, "I will prevent it with this force of soldiers." Indeed, the name "saṅgara" is a name for making friends, giving bribes, and gathering troops. Therefore, this meaning is spoken.
171:
There is no 'saṅgara' (commitment/association) in the sense of forming a friendship, saying 'I will do it'; nor in the sense of giving a bribe, saying 'Take this hundred or thousand and wait for a few days'; nor in the sense of gathering an army, saying 'I will resist with this force of soldiers.' Since 'saṅgara' is a name for forming friendships, giving bribes, and gathering armies, this meaning is spoken.

'Atanditaṃ' means being free from laziness and endowed with energetic effort. Because of practicing in this way, one has an auspicious night; therefore, he is called 'Bhaddékaratta.' The Buddha-muni, who is peaceful because of the subsiding of passion and so on, declares such a person as 'This one is a Bhaddékaratta.'

In the passages beginning with 'evaṃrūpo' (of such a form), the meaning is: even if the complexion was dark, it was like the color of an indanīla (sapphire) gem; thus, in the sense of a pleasant form, it means 'I had such a rūpakkhandha.' In the sense of wholesome pleasant feeling and mental joy, it means 'I had such a vedanākkhandha.' In the sense of perception and so on associated with those feelings, it means 'In the past, I had such saññā, such saṅkhāra, and such viññāṇa.'

Following after and giving rise to craving in those (past) aggregates like rūpa is called 'nandiṃ samanvāneti' (following after delight). However, one does not consider 'I had such a rūpakkhandha... such a viññāṇa' in the sense of inferior forms and so on.

Not following after and not giving rise to craving or the views associated with craving is called 'nandiṃ na samanvāneti.'

In the passages beginning with 'evaṃrūpo siyaṃ' (might I be of such a form), the arising of delight and wrong view, described as the occurrence of craving and views in the sense of those pleasant forms and so on, should also be understood.

'Bhikkhus, how is one pulled away (saṃhīrati) among present states?' This is spoken to explain the meaning of the summary (uddesa): 'He sees the present state in each place; he is not pulled away (asaṃhīra), he is not shaken (asaṃkuppa).' Indeed, although it should have been said here, 'Bhikkhus, how does one not practice insight (vipassanā) into present states?', because insight is spoken of as 'asaṃhīra' and 'asaṃkuppa,' the Buddha extracted the heading (mātikā) 'saṃhīrati' and explained it in detail to show the absence and presence of that insight. In that heading, 'saṃhīrati' means being pulled away by craving and views toward the ocean of the four woeful states or the ocean of saṃsāra due to the absence of insight.
172:
Craving and views pull one away (to the ocean of saṃsāra). 'Na saṃhīrati' means not being pulled away by craving and views due to the development of insight. The remaining words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## 2. Commentary on the Ānanda-bhaddékaratta Sutta
'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Ānanda-bhaddékaratta Sutta. Therein, 'arisen from seclusion' (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito) means arisen from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). 'Bhikkhus, who is it?'—He asked this for the purpose of initiating a conversation, even though He already knew.

'Sādhu sādhu'—He gave the cry of 'Sādhu' (well done) to the Elder Ānanda. 'You are good'—He said this while praising the teaching because it was spoken with well-rounded, pure words and syllables. The remaining words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## 3. Commentary on the Mahākaccāna-bhaddékaratta Sutta
'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Mahākaccāna-bhaddékaratta Sutta. Therein, 'Tapodārāma' refers to the monastery that received this name because of the lake with hot water. It is said that beneath Mount Vebhāra, there is a Naga realm of five hundred yojanas belonging to the earth-dwelling Nagas, which is like the celestial realm, endowed with gem-paved grounds and park-gardens. In the playing area of the Nagas there, there is a large lake of water, from which the river named Tapodā flows with boiling hot water. Why did it become like this? It is said that a great realm of hungry ghosts (peta) surrounds the city of Rājagaha; this Tapodā river flows between two great Lohakumbhī hells, and therefore it flows boiling hot. This was also said: 'Bhikkhus, that lake from which this Tapodā river flows has clear water, cool water, delicious water, pure water, with good banks, and is delightful, with many fish and turtles, and lotuses the size of chariot wheels...'
173:
"Monks, indeed this Tapodā River flows between two great hells; therefore, this Tapodā River flows boiling hot," it is stated (in the Pārājika Pali). Directly in front of this Tapodā monastery, there is a large lake formed from that river; this monastery is called 'Tapodārāma' after the name of that lake.

'Samiddhi' means that the Elder's physical body was perfect, beautiful, and inspiring; thus, he came to be known simply as 'Samiddhi'. 'Ādibrahmacariyaka' means being the preliminary practice that is the beginning of the holy life of the Path. The passage beginning with "Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat..." should be understood in detail as explained in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta.

In this sutta, beginning with "Thus my eye...", the Blessed One set forth the Mātikā (outline) solely by way of the twelve Āyatanas (sense bases). The Elder, having grasped the method, said: "The Blessed One has provided the Mātikā and the Vibhaṅga (analysis) by way of the five aggregates in the two suttas below (Bhaddekaratta and Ānanda Bhaddekaratta) and in the fourth sutta above (Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddekaratta); however, in this sutta, the Mātikā is set forth for analysis solely by way of the twelve Āyatanas." The Elder, in obtaining this method, performed a difficult task; it is like showing a footprint where no footprint exists, or like making a footprint in the sky. Therefore, the Blessed One, referring to this very sutta, placed him in the position of Etadagga (foremost), saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who analyze in detail the meaning of what I have spoken in brief, this Mahākaccāna is the foremost."

In this context, 'Cakkhu' refers to visual sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). 'Rūpā' refers to visible objects produced by the four causes (catu-samuṭṭhānika). The remaining Āyatanas should be understood in this same manner. 'Viññāṇa' refers to consciousness accompanied by attachment (nikanti-viññāṇa). 'Tadabhinandati' means greatly delighting in that eye and visible object through the power of craving and views. 'Anvāgameti' means following along with craving and views.

In the passage "Thus my mind was in the past, thus were the phenomena...", 'Mano' refers to the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta). 'Dhammā' refers to the mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) belonging to the three planes.

'Paṇidahati' means placing by way of aspiration. 'Paṇidhānapaccayā' means because of the cause of placing through aspiration. The remaining terms are clear in all places.

174:
## 4. Commentary on the Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Thus have I heard" is the Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, 'Lomasakaṅgiya' is understood to be the name of this Elder, Aṅga; he became well-known as Lomasakaṅgiya because his body had a slight hairiness. 'Candana Devaputta' refers to a lay follower named Candana during the time of Kassapa Buddha, who was wealthy and possessed great riches; having honored the Three Jewels with the four requisites, he was reborn in the celestial realm and became known as Candana Devaputta, following his previous name. 'Paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ' means on a stone slab like a red blanket. The color of that stone slab is said to be like a red blanket or like a cluster of jayasumana flowers; therefore, it is called "Paṇḍukambalasilā".

When did the Blessed One stay there? In the seventh year after attaining Buddhahood, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the city of Sāvatthī, having performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire in the midst of an assembly spanning twelve yojanas, he descended from the sky and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree. By preaching the Dhamma, he rescued the great multitude from the vast whirlpool of saṃsāra. Since Buddhas do not stay on the paths of humans after performing miracles, he took a stride while the people were still watching and entered the rains-retreat on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It was at that time he stayed there.

"There the Blessed One" means the Blessed One, while staying there, was mostly surrounded by deities and Brahmas who had assembled from ten thousand world-systems. While teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, taking his mother (reborn as a deity) as the witness, he taught the summary (uddesa) and analysis (vibhaṅga) of the Bhaddekaratta Sutta at intervals to arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in those deities who were unable to penetrate the deep and subtle discourse that distinguishes mind and matter, characterized by the three marks. In that assembly of deities, this Candana Devaputta, while learning, learned these verses along with the detailed analysis. However, because the state of a deity is a ground for negligence, being oppressed by celestial sense-objects, he gradually forgot the text of the sutta and retained only the verses. Therefore, he said: "Bhikkhu, I remember the Bhaddekaratta verses thus."
175:
In the words beginning with "Learn," one who listens in silence and learns is said to "uggaṇhāti" (learns). One who recites and chants orally is said to "pariyāpuṇāti" (masters/studies). One who teaches others is said to "dhāreti" (bears/retains). The rest of the words are clear in meaning.

## 5. Explanation of the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta

In the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," the name "Subha" refers to that young man who was handsome and inspiring to look at; therefore, because of his physical beauty, they named him "Subha" (Beautiful). As for "Māṇava" (Young Man), he was called so in his youth, and even in his old age, he was still addressed by that term. "Todeyyaputta" means he was the son of the Brahmin Todeyya, the chaplain (purohita) of King Pasenadi. That Todeyya was known as such because he was the lord of the village of Tudi, not far from Sāvatthī. He was very wealthy, possessing a fortune of 870 million (87 crores), but he was extremely stingy. Thinking, "If I give, my wealth will be exhausted," he gave nothing to anyone. It is also said:

"Seeing the depletion of collyrium,
And the growth of anthills,
And the gathering of honey by bees,
A wise man should dwell in the household life."

In this way, he taught only non-giving. Without giving even a ladle of gruel or a spoonful of rice to the Fully Enlightened One who resided in the nearby monastery, he died with greed for wealth and was reborn as a dog in that very house. Subha the young man loved that dog exceedingly, feeding it the same food he ate himself and letting it sleep on a noble bed.

Then, one day at dawn, the Blessed One, while surveying the world, saw that dog. He realized: "The Brahmin Todeyya, through greed for wealth, has been reborn as a dog in his own house. Today, when I go to Subha's house, the dog will bark at me. Then I will say one word to it. At that, the dog will think, 'The ascetic Gotama knows me,' and will go to lie down in a quiet place. Because of that, Subha and I will have a conversation, and Subha will be established in the Refuges." Furthermore, He saw that the dog, after death, would be reborn in hell. Knowing that Subha would be established in the Refuges, the Blessed One, after attending to His physical needs that day, entered Subha's house for alms at the time of the alms-round, just as Subha was going out.
176:
The dog will lie down in the place where the stove-stand is. Because of that act of lying down, Subha the young man will have the opportunity to converse with me. Having heard the Dhamma, Subha will be established in the Refuges. The dog, however, will be reborn in hell after death. Knowing that the young man would be established in the Refuges, the Blessed One, after performing His morning duties, entered the village alone and went into the house for alms after the young man had departed.

Upon seeing the Blessed One, the dog barked and approached Him. Then the Blessed One said to the dog: "Todeyya, in the past you were reborn as a dog because you insulted me by saying 'Bho, Bho.' Now, if you bark again, you will go to the Avīci hell." Hearing this, the dog felt remorseful, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama knows me," and with its head bowed, it went to lie in the hot ashes between the stove-stand. The people were unable to lift it back onto the bed. When Subha returned, he asked, "Who took this dog down from the bed?" The people said that no one had done so and related the whole incident. Hearing this, the young man was angry, thinking: "My father is reborn in the Brahma world; there can be no dog named Todeyya. The ascetic Gotama is calling my father a dog; he says whatever comes to his mouth." Desiring to refute the Blessed One for lying, he went to the monastery and asked about the matter.

The Blessed One told him exactly what He had said to the dog, and to show that it was not false, He asked: "Young man, is there any wealth that your father did not tell you about?" "Master Gotama, there is a gold necklace worth a hundred thousand, gold sandals worth a hundred thousand, a gold bowl worth a hundred thousand, and a hundred thousand coins," he replied. "Go, feed that dog thick milk-rice (ghana-pāyāsa), place it on the bed, and when it has fallen slightly asleep, ask it. It will tell you everything. Then you will know, 'This is my father.'" The young man was pleased for two reasons: "If it is true, I will get the wealth; if not, I will refute the ascetic Gotama for lying." He went and did as instructed.

The dog, thinking "I am known by this person," cried out, made a "hum hum" sound, went to the place where the wealth was buried, and gave a sign by scratching the earth with its paws. When the young man obtained the wealth, he thought: "The transition between births is so subtle, yet it is clear to the ascetic Gotama. Truly, he is omniscient." With a heart full of confidence in the Blessed One, he prepared fourteen questions. It is said that this young man was an expert in the science of limbs (aṅgavijjā).
177:
Subha the young man had this thought: "I will take this gift of Dhamma and ask the ascetic Gotama these questions." Thus, on his second visit, he approached the Blessed One. Regarding the questions asked by Subha the young man, the Blessed One, wishing to answer them all at once, spoke the words beginning with 'Kammassakā'.

In that passage, the meaning is: Beings are 'Kammassakā' because kamma is their own property. They are 'Kammadāyādā' because they are the heirs of kamma; it means kamma is their inheritance and property. They are 'Kammayonī' because kamma is their origin or cause. They are 'Kammabandhū' because kamma is their kin; it means kamma is their relative. They are 'Kammapaṭisaraṇā' because kamma is their refuge and foundation.

Regarding the phrase 'yadidaṃ hīnapraṇītatāya' (this distinction between the inferior and the superior): it means that this division into inferior and superior—such as 'you be inferior, you be superior; you be short-lived, you be long-lived... you be of little wisdom, you be wise'—is not made by anyone else; kamma alone distinguishes beings in this way.

Subha the young man was unable to understand the meaning of the words spoken. It was as if a sweet meal had been placed before someone whose face was bound with a thick cloth. This young man was one who relied on pride, considering himself a scholar, and did not see anyone as his equal. Then, the Blessed One thought: "Lest he should have the pride of thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is only saying what I already know,' I will speak by making it difficult to penetrate from the start. Then he will entreat me, saying, 'Venerable Gotama, I do not understand; please explain it to me clearly in detail.' When he thus entreats me, I will speak; in this way, it will be beneficial for him." Thinking thus, He spoke by making it difficult to penetrate. Now, Subha the young man, wishing to reveal his lack of penetration, spoke the words beginning with 'Na kho ahaṃ'.

'Samattena' means with completeness. 'Samādinnena' means by having accepted or grasped. 'Appāyukasaṃvattanikā esā māṇava paṭipadā yadidaṃ pāṇātipātī' means: "Young man, this practice of killing living beings is a practice that leads to a short life."

How does this killing of living beings cause a short life? There are four types of kamma: Upapīḷaka (oppressing kamma), Upacchedaka (destructive kamma), Janaka (productive kamma), and Upatthambhaka (supportive kamma). Upapīḷaka kamma oppresses a being who has been reborn through a powerful kamma during the course of existence (pavattikāla). That kamma says, as it were: "If I, the unwholesome kamma, had known earlier, I would not have given you the opportunity to be born in such a happy destination or a wealthy family, but would have caused you to be born only in the four woeful states. Now that you have already been born somewhere, I will oppress you who are born, making you devoid of essence, vitality, and substance." Thus, it causes many dangers and the destruction of wealth. From the moment the child is conceived in the mother's womb, the mother feels no pleasure or happiness, and only suffering arises for the parents.
178:
That unwholesome kamma comes and speaks thus in essence: "If I had known earlier, I would not have allowed you to be born in this life; I would have caused you to be born only in the four woeful states. Let it be, wherever you are born, I, being the one called Upapīḷaka kamma, will oppress you and make you devoid of essence, vitality, and substance." From that time on, it makes that being into such a state. How does it do so? It brings about dangers and causes the destruction of wealth and possessions.

In doing so, from the time the child is conceived in the mother's womb, the mother no longer has enjoyment or happiness, and only the oppression (suffering) of the parents arises. In this way, it brings about danger. Furthermore, from the time the child is born in the mother's womb, the wealth in the house perishes through the power of kings and others, like salt that has reached water. Cows that used to give a potful of milk no longer give milk. Gentle oxen become fierce, go blind, or become hunchbacked. Disease falls upon the herd of cattle. Servants and others do not obey orders. Sown crops do not grow. Wealth that has reached the house perishes in the house; wealth in the forest perishes in the forest. Gradually, even obtaining mere food and clothing becomes difficult. There can be no proper care for the pregnancy. At the time of birth, the mother's milk fails. The child, receiving no care and being oppressed, becomes devoid of essence, vitality, and substance. This is called Upapīḷaka kamma.

However, for a being born through kamma that leads to a long life, Upacchedaka kamma comes and cuts off the life-span. For example, just as if a man were to shoot an arrow to reach a distance of eight usabhas, and another person were to strike that arrow just as it was released from the bow with a club, causing it to fall right there; similarly, Upacchedaka kamma cuts off the life-span of a being born through kamma that leads to a long life. How does it do so? It causes one to enter a forest inhabited by robbers, or to fall into water with fierce crocodiles, or brings one to some other dangerous place. This is called Upacchedaka kamma; 'Upaghātaka kamma' is also a name for this same kamma.

Kamma that produces rebirth is called Janaka kamma. Kamma that supports a being born into a family of little wealth and so on, by providing the fulfillment of wealth and possessions, is called Upatthambhaka kamma.

Among these four, the first two are only unwholesome. Janaka kamma can be both wholesome and unwholesome. Upatthambhaka kamma is only wholesome. Among those, the kamma of killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) leads to a short life as Upacchedaka kamma. Or, that which is done by one who kills living beings...
179:
In another way, the wholesome karma of a person who commits the act of killing (pāṇātipāta) is not grand; it is unable to produce a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) associated with a long life. Thus, the act of killing leads to a short life. Alternatively, it determines the rebirth-linking itself to be short-lived, thereby making the life short. Or, due to the decisive intention (sanniṭṭhāna-cetanā), one is reborn in hell; and due to the preceding and succeeding intentions (pubbāparacetanā), one becomes short-lived in the manner already described.

In this Sutta, regarding the statement, "Young man, this is the practice that leads to longevity," even for a being born due to minor unwholesome karma, the wholesome karma of refraining from killing arrives during the course of existence (pavatti) and, in terms of its significance, speaks thus: "If I had known earlier, I would not have allowed you to be born here; I would have caused you to be born only in the celestial realm. Let it be; wherever you may be born, I will provide you with support like a pillar, known as supportive karma (upatthambhaka-kamma)." Thus, it provides support. How does it do so? It destroys dangers and brings about wealth and possessions.

In that regard, from the time the child is conceived in the mother's womb, only happiness and pleasantness occur for the parents. All natural dangers, such as those from humans and non-humans (amanussa), disappear. In this way, it destroys dangers. Furthermore, from the time the child is conceived in the mother's womb, there is no limit to the wealth in the house; pots of gold come rolling into the house from both the front and the back. The parents come to possess even the wealth deposited by others. Cows produce much milk, oxen are of good temperament, and crops abound in the fields. Wealth that was to be paid with interest or borrowed temporarily is brought and given voluntarily without being asked. Servants and others are easy to admonish, and business activities do not decline. From the time he is in the womb, the child receives care, and pediatricians are always present. One born in a householder's family attains the position of a Seṭṭhi; one born in a ministerial family or similar attains the position of a general (senāpati) and so on. In this way, it brings about wealth and possessions. That person, free from danger and endowed with wealth, lives for a long time. Thus, the karma of refraining from killing leads to longevity.

Alternatively, other wholesome deeds performed by one who refrains from killing also become grand and are able to produce a rebirth-linking associated with a long life; in this way too, it leads to longevity. Or, it determines the rebirth-linking itself to be long-lived, thereby making the life long. Or, due to the decisive intention, one is reborn in the celestial realm; and due to the preceding and succeeding intentions, one becomes long-lived in the manner already described. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all the answers to the questions.
180:
Indeed, when the karma of harming (viheṭhana) and so forth arises during the course of existence, it is as if it speaks in the same manner in terms of its significance: by causing oppression, it leads to a state of being without wealth, and due to not receiving care, it causes the occurrence of diseases and so forth. This happens either because of the lack of grandness in the wholesome karma performed by the harmer and so forth, or by determining the rebirth-linking from the very beginning, or by the power of the preceding and succeeding intentions in the manner already described, leading to much sickness (bahvābādha) and so forth. Just as refraining from killing leads to health, so too non-harming (aviheṭhana) and so forth lead to the state of having little sickness (appābādha) and so forth.

In this context, "issāmanako" means one whose mind is associated with envy (issā). "Upadussatī" means offending (through the ten grounds of insult) by the power of envy itself. "Issāṃ bandhatī" means keeping envy as if binding it, like binding a sheaf of barley so that it does not get lost. "Appesakkho" means one with few followers or little influence; such a person is not prominent, like an arrow shot in the night; even when sitting and washing hands after a meal, he cannot even find someone to give him water.

"Na dātā hoti" means not being a giver due to the power of stinginess (macchariya). "Te na kammena" means because of that karma of stinginess.

"Abhīvādetabbaṃ" refers to the Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a Noble Disciple (ariyasāvaka) who is worthy of salutation. The same principle applies to rising to greet (paccuṭṭhāna) and so forth. However, in answering this question, oppressive karma (upapīḷaka-kamma) and supportive karma (upatthambhaka-kamma) should not be taken. Indeed, during the course of existence (pavatti), it is not possible to make one of low birth into one of high birth or vice versa. Only at the time of rebirth-linking is it determined: karma that leads to low birth causes rebirth in a low family, and karma that leads to high birth causes rebirth in a high family.

Regarding the phrase "na paripucchitā hoti," one does not be reborn in hell merely by not asking questions. However, one who does not ask questions does not know, "This should be done, this should not be done." Not knowing, he fails to do what should be done and does what should not be done. Because of such actions, he is reborn in hell, while the other (who asks) is reborn in heaven. Thus, the Teacher led the discourse to its conclusion according to the sequence, saying, "Thus, young man, [it is due to this cause] that there is inferiority and excellence." The rest of the text is clear in all places.

## The Explanation of the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## It is also called the Subha Sutta.
181:
## 6. Mahākammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta. In that sutta, "mogha" means empty or fruitless. "Sacca" means that which is true and manifest. This wanderer Potaliputta had not heard these words about "mogha" (referring to bodily, verbal, and mental action) and "sacca" directly from the Blessed One. However, in the Upāli Sutta, the Blessed One said: "I designate mental action as being more blameworthy for the performance of evil deeds and for the occurrence of evil deeds, and not so much bodily action or verbal action." This statement became well-known among the sectarians, and taking hold of that statement, this wanderer speaks. The statement "That attainment exists" is spoken in reference to the discussion on the cessation of higher perception (abhisannānirodhakathā) that arose in the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta: "How then, sir, does the cessation of higher perception occur?" "Does not feel anything" means not feeling even a single type of feeling. When the Elder Samiddhi admits, "It exists," he does so in reference to the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). "Should be protected" means it should be protected so as to be free from reproach. Because there is volition (cetanā), it is called "sañcetanika" (volitional). It means having performed a volitional action along with intention. The Elder's statement "That person is suffering" was said with the perception that "the wanderer is asking only with reference to unwholesome [actions]."

When the Blessed One said, "I too have seen," it means that the Blessed One, even in fourfold darkness, can see with his physical eye (maṃsacakkhu) a formation (saṅkhāra) as small as a sesame seed within a radius of one league. This wanderer lives in a place only about a gāvuta away. Why then did the Blessed One speak thus? He said it in reference to having seen him in a public gathering.

"Udāyī" refers to Lāḷudāyī. "In that suffering" means all that is just suffering. Thus, in reference to the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha), the suffering of defilements (kilesadukkha), and the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkha), he means: "If the Blessed One had spoken [thus], the Elder Samiddhi's answer would be appropriate."

"Ummanga" is the emergence of a question. "Ummujjāmāna" means sticking out the head. "He will emerge improperly" means he will stick out his head without a proper method. The Blessed One knew this not through the divine eye, the knowledge of others' minds, or omniscience, but he knew it through [Udāyī's] intention and demeanor. Indeed, the intention of one who is about to speak is easy to know; one who wishes to speak stretches his neck, moves his jaw, his face twitches, and he cannot sit still. Seeing Udāyī's demeanor, the Blessed One reflected, "This Udāyī cannot sit still; he will surely speak what is not true," and thus knew it by his intention.
182:
Seeing his demeanor, [the Blessed One] knew just by looking: "This Udāyī cannot sit still; he will surely speak what is not true." "Ādiṃ yevā" means only at the beginning. "Tisso vedanā" (three feelings) means that the wanderer Potaliputta, when asking "What does that person feel?", asked about the three feelings by specifically defining them as "I ask about the three feelings." "Sukhavedaniya" refers to the kamma that is the cause of pleasant feeling. In the remaining terms, the method should be understood in the same way.

In this context, the four volitions associated with consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa) from sense-sphere wholesome [kamma], and the volitions of the three lower jhānas mentioned below, are called pleasant-feeling kamma (sukhavedaniya kamma) because they produce pleasant feeling at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. Among these, sense-sphere wholesome [kamma] produces only pleasure at rebirth-linking; during the course of existence, it also produces neutral feeling (upekkhā) toward desirable-neutral objects.

Unwholesome volition (akusala cetanā) is called painful-feeling kamma (dukkhavedaniya kamma) because it produces only suffering at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. This kamma produces only pain when it occurs at the body-door; elsewhere, it also produces neutral feeling. However, because that feeling arises only toward undesirable objects, it is reckoned simply as "suffering."

The four volitions associated with consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā) from sense-sphere wholesome [kamma], and the fourth jhāna volition from fine-material sphere wholesome [kamma], are called neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling kamma (adukkhamasukhavedaniya kamma) because they produce the third feeling (equanimity) at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. Here, the four sense-sphere wholesome equanimity volitions produce only neutral feeling at rebirth-linking; during the course of existence, they also produce pleasant feeling toward desirable objects. Furthermore, pleasant-feeling kamma is appropriate in terms of rebirth-linking and the course of existence; likewise, neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling kamma is appropriate. Painful-feeling kamma, however, is appropriate only in terms of the course of existence. But by the power of this painful-feeling kamma, all [three types of] kamma are appropriate in terms of the course of existence.

"Etassa Bhagavā" means that the Elder Ānanda, seeing that the Tathāgata wished to speak the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta, and thinking "I will make the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Action manifest to the Saṅgha of monks by requesting the Tathāgata," spoke thus, being skilled in connecting the discourse. In that context, "Mahākammavibhaṅga" means the analysis of many actions. "Ananda, what are the four... here, Ananda, a certain person... is reborn in hell"—this statement is not yet the analysis of the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Action, but is the setting down of the matrix (mātikā) for the purpose of analyzing the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Action.
183:
Venerable Ānanda, the words 'Here, some ascetic...' are a separate connection. The Blessed One undertook this discourse to show that 'ascetics and brahmins with the divine eye, having made this an object and obtained this cause, hold this view.' Therein, the five terms beginning with 'ardor' (ātappa) are just names for energy (vīriya). 'Concentration of mind' (cetosamādhi) means the concentration of the divine eye. 'He sees' (passati) means he sees when observing, 'Where has that being been reborn?' It means that the knowledge of those ascetics and brahmins who know, 'Because of fulfilling the ten wholesome courses of action, one is reborn in hell,' is wrong. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sections. 'Viditaṃ' means being evident. 'Thāmasa' means by the power of [wrong] view. 'Parāmāsa' means misapprehension through [wrong] view. 'Abhinivissa voharati' means speaking after having firmly adhered to and taken up [a view].

Ānanda, these words 'among those four ascetics and brahmins' are not yet the analysis of the Great Analysis of Kamma (Mahākammavibhaṅga-ñāṇa), but merely the laying down of the matrix (mātikā) of that knowledge. Here, in the words of those with the divine eye, it is shown that 'this much is allowed, and this much is not allowed.' Therein, 'tatra' means among those four ascetics and brahmins. 'Idamassa' means this statement is his. 'Aññathā' means in another way. Thus, in the doctrine of those ascetics and brahmins, it should be understood that in two places it is allowed and in three places it is not allowed; thus, the allowance and non-allowance in all places should be known.

Having thus shown the allowance and non-allowance in the words of those with the divine eye, now, wishing to analyze the Great Analysis of Kamma, He said: 'Ānanda, among those four persons, the one who...' and so forth.

'Or previously that kamma was done by him' means the kamma done before the kamma seen by the one with the divine eye. One is reborn in hell because of kamma done previously, or because of kamma done later, or at the time of death because of wrong views such as 'Khanda is supreme, Siva is supreme, the Great Brahma is supreme, or the world was created by Issara and others.' 'In this very life' means that among those kammas, if it is kamma to be experienced in this life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya), he experiences the result in this very life; if it is kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya), after being reborn; if it is kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya), in a subsequent turn.
184:
Thus, this ascetic or brahmin who has attained the divine eye sees one heap of kamma and one heap of result. The Blessed One, however, sees the three heaps of kamma and two heaps of result that this person does not see. Furthermore, the Blessed One sees the four heaps of kamma and three heaps of result, both seen and unseen by this person. The knowledge that knows these seven points is called the Tathāgata's Great Analysis of Kamma. In the second section, the person with the divine eye sees nothing at all, but the Blessed One sees three heaps of kamma and two heaps of result. The knowledge that knows these five points known by Himself is also called the Tathāgata's Great Analysis of Kamma. The same method applies to the remaining two sections.

'Abhabba' is unwholesome kamma devoid of reality. 'Abhabbābhāsa' has the meaning of suppressing and preventing [weak] unwholesome kamma. When much unwholesome kamma is accumulated, a strong kamma prevents the result of a weak kamma and makes an opportunity for its own result; this kamma is called both 'abhabba' and 'abhabbābhāsa'. If, after accumulating wholesome kamma, unwholesome kamma is done at the time of death, that unwholesome kamma prevents the result of the wholesome kamma and makes an opportunity for its own result; this kamma is called both 'abhabba' and 'bhabbābhāsa'. Even when much wholesome kamma is accumulated, a strong kamma prevents the result of a weak kamma and makes an opportunity for its own result; this kamma is called both 'bhabba' and 'bhabbābhāsa'. If, after accumulating unwholesome kamma, wholesome kamma is done at the time of death, that wholesome kamma prevents the result of the unwholesome kamma and makes an opportunity for its own result; this kamma is called both 'bhabba' and 'abhabbābhāsa'.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood here by the manner of appearance. It is called 'abhabbābhāsa' because it appears as 'abhabba'. Among those four persons, four types of persons are mentioned in the manner beginning with 'Here, a certain person is one who takes life'. Among them, the kamma of the first person is called both 'abhabba' and 'abhabbābhāsa'. That kamma is called 'abhabba' because it is unwholesome; because that person is reborn in hell, it appears as the unwholesome kamma that is the cause of rebirth in hell. The kamma of the second person is called both 'abhabba' and 'bhabbābhāsa'. That kamma is called 'abhabba' because it is unwholesome. Because that person is reborn in heaven, for the other sectarians, rebirth in heaven...
185:
Wholesome kamma, which is the cause of rebirth (in the celestial realm), arises and appears. The same method should be understood for the remaining two types of kamma. All other remaining words are clear and easy to understand in every instance.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta

"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, "to be known" (veditabbāni) refers to things that should be known by the Path-knowledge along with insight (by way of discerning the object and non-delusion). "Mental explorations" (manopavicārā) refers to initial and sustained thoughts (vitakka-vicāra). Here, "mind" (mano) is intended as the consciousness that gives rise to initial thought; because they wander near that mind, they are called "mental explorations" (manopavicāra). "Steps for beings" (sattapadā) refers to the practices or causes of practice for beings who are dependent on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). In this sutta, there are 18 factors of the round (vaṭṭapada) and 18 factors of the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭapada); these should also be known only by the Path-knowledge along with insight. "For trainers" (yoggācariyānaṃ) means teachers who teach the arts of elephant training and so forth, or teachers who tame those who should be tamed. The remaining meaning will be made clear in the Vibhaṅga Pali. "This summary" (ayam uddeso) refers to the setting down of this table of contents (mātikā).

The eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. "Eye-consciousness" (cakkhuviññāṇaṃ) refers to the two types of eye-consciousness by way of wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. The same method should be understood for the consciousnesses dependent on the remaining sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa). Excluding these ten types of sense-consciousness (dvipañcaviññāṇa), the remaining consciousness (along with the mind-element) is called "mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa) here.

"Eye-contact" (cakkhusamphasso) is the contact (phassa) occurring at the eye-sensitivity. It is a designation for the contact associated with eye-consciousness. The same method should be understood for the remaining ear-contact and so forth.

"Having seen a form with the eye" (cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā) means having seen a visible object with eye-consciousness. This method applies everywhere. "Basis for joy" (somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ) refers to a visible object that is the cause for the arising of pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā) by way of the object. "Explores" (upavicarati) means one investigates by the occurrence of sustained thought (vicāra) on that object; initial thought (vitakka) is also associated with that sustained thought. In this way, the 18 mental explorations known as initial and sustained thoughts should be understood. In the phrase "six explorations accompanied by joy" (cha somanassūpavicārā), they are called "explorations accompanied by joy" because they wander and investigate together with pleasant feeling. The same method should be understood for the remaining two terms.
186:
"Household-based" (gehasita) refers to things dependent on the cords of sensual pleasure. "Renunciation-based" (nekkhamma-sita) refers to things dependent on insight (vipassanā). "Desirable" (iṭṭha) refers to objects that are sought after. "Lovely" (kanta) refers to objects that are desired. "Pleasing to the mind" (manorama) means they are called pleasing because the mind delights in those objects; it refers to objects that are the site of the mind's delight. "Connected with worldly baits" (lokāmisa-paṭisaṃyutta) refers to things connected with craving (taṇhā). "Past" (atīta) refers to objects already obtained. Let joy arise by taking a present object as the focus; how can it arise in the past? Even in the past, strong joy arises for a person who recollects, "Just as I now experience a desirable object, so too did I experience one in the past."

"Impermanence" (aniccatā) refers to the nature of being impermanent. "Change, fading away, and cessation" (vipariṇāma virāga nirodha) mean change by abandoning the natural state, fading away by disappearing, and cessation by ceasing. "Right wisdom" (sammappaññā) refers to insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). This is called "renunciation-based joy." Just as joy arises for a king looking at the perfection of his own glory, the joy that arises for a yogi who sits practicing insight, seeing the breaking up of formations (saṅkhāra), while the sharp and mature insight-knowledge proceeds regarding those formations, is called "renunciation-based joy." This has also been said:

"For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty place, whose mind is peaceful, and who clearly sees the Dhamma with insight, there is a delight that transcends that of humans.
Whenever he contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, he gains rapture and joy; for those who know, that is the Deathless."

"These six" refers to the six types of renunciation-based joy that arise for a person who sits practicing insight by way of impermanence and so forth when a desirable object comes into range at the six doors.

Regarding "past": let grief (domanassa) arise for a person who longs for the present but does not obtain it; how can it arise in the past? Even in the past, strong grief arises for a person who recollects, "Just as I now long for a desirable object and do not obtain it, so too did I long for one in the past and did not obtain it."

"Unsurpassed liberations" (anuttara-vimokkha) refers to the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala); it means for one who directs an aspiration toward Arahatship. "Base" (āyatana) refers to the base that is the fruit of Arahatship. "For one establishing a longing" (pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato) means for one who directs an aspiration. That aspiration...
187: Because it has longing (taṇhā) as its root, it is said: 'pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato' (for one who arouses longing). These six types of grief based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita domanassa) should be understood as the grief that arises through the flow of tears, like that of the Elder Mahāsīva, a resident of Gāmantapabbhāra, who lamented, 'I have not been able to reach the fruit of Arahatship throughout this week, this month, and this whole year,' when he was unable to exert effort after arousing longing for Arahatship and establishing insight through the perception of impermanence and so forth when a pleasant object appeared at the six doors. The detailed story of that Elder is mentioned in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, known as the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī; those who wish to know may take it from there. In the phrase 'uppajjati upekkhā' (equanimity arises), equanimity refers to the equanimity of ignorance (aññāṇupekkhā). One who has conquered the limit of defilements is called an 'Odhijina' (conqueror of limits), which refers to an Arahant; therefore, 'Anodhijina' means a non-Arahant (worldling). One who has conquered future results (vipāka) is also called a 'Vipākajina' (conqueror of results), which refers to an Arahant; therefore, 'Avipākajina' means a non-Arahant, including both trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana). One who does not see things in terms of danger or disadvantage is called 'Anādīnavadassāvī'. These six types of equanimity based on the household life (gehasita upekkhā) should be understood as the equanimity that arises when a pleasant object appears at the six doors, being stuck and attached to those objects like flies stuck to a lump of molasses, unable to transcend forms and so forth. 'Rūpaṃ sā ativattati' means that renunciation-based equanimity does not transcend the form (it contemplates it with insight) and does not remain there through the power of desire. These six types of equanimity based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita upekkhā) should be understood as the equanimity associated with insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that arises when pleasant or other objects appear at the six doors, without lusting for the pleasant, without hating the unpleasant, and without being deluded in improper contemplation. 'Tatra idaṃ nissāya idaṃ pajahatha' (Therein, by relying on this, abandon that) means that among those thirty-six tracks of beings (sattapada), one should abandon eighteen by relying on eighteen. For this reason, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, therein, those six types of renunciation-based (joy)...' and so forth. 'Nissāya āgamma' means relying on by way of occurrence and coming as a support. In this way, by the arising of renunciation-based joy, one transcends household-based joy. After causing the abandonment of household-based joy by means of similar renunciation-based joy, the Blessed One now spoke the words 'Tatra bhikkhave yāni cha nekkhammasitāni somanassāni' and so forth, wishing to cause the abandonment of weak states by means of strong renunciation-based joy. Thus, by means of renunciation-based joy, one abandons renunciation-based grief; and by means of renunciation-based equanimity, one abandons renunciation-based joy. The abandonment of the weak by the strong is thus taught. In brief, the explanation of the Pali sequence is paused here, and the discourse on equanimity is explained in detail. For the four types of monks who practice insight based on the three jhānas—the first, second, and third—and on pure formations (suddha-saṅkhāra), the preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā)...
188:
In this way, by the occurrence of renunciation-based states, the household-based states are said to be transcended.

After causing the abandonment of similar household-based joy by means of similar renunciation-based joy, the Blessed One now spoke the words: 'Bhikkhus, therein, those six types of renunciation-based joy...' and so forth, wishing to cause the abandonment of weak states by means of strong states. Thus, by causing the abandonment of renunciation-based grief through renunciation-based joy, and renunciation-based joy through renunciation-based equanimity, the abandonment of the weak by the strong is taught.

At this point, the discourse on equanimity should be understood. Among the eight attainments (samāpatti), for the four types of monks who begin insight by taking the first three jhānas or pure formations as a basis, the preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) preceding the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) may be accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity. However, the insight leading to emergence is accompanied only by joy. For the five types of monks who begin insight by taking the fourth jhāna and so forth as a basis, the preliminary insight is the same as mentioned before. However, the insight leading to emergence is accompanied by equanimity. With reference to this insight leading to emergence, it was said: 'By relying on the six renunciation-based equanimities, by depending on them, abandon the six renunciation-based joys.' For a monk who practices in this way, not only does this specific feeling (vedanā) occur in insight, but there is also a distinction in the factors of jhāna, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the path factors (maggaṅga) in the Noble Path.

What determines this distinction? Some Elders say that the jhāna used as a basis for insight (pādakajjhāna) determines it. Some say the aggregates (khandha) that are the objects of insight determine it. Others say the individual's disposition (ajjhāsaya) determines it. Even in the views of those Elders, it should be understood that only this insight leading to emergence in the preliminary stage determines it. The definitive explanation on this matter has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the description of equanimity regarding formations (Saṅkhārupekkhā-niddesa).

'Nānatta' (diversity) means various, many, and of manifold kinds. 'Nānattasita' (based on diversity) means relying on various objects. 'Ekatta' (unity) means being of a single nature. 'Ekattasita' (based on unity) means relying on a single object. What is this equanimity? Previously, the equanimity of ignorance (aññāṇupekkhā) was mentioned; later, the six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) will be mentioned. Here, two types of equanimity are taken: equanimity of serenity (samatha-upekkhā) and equanimity of insight (vipassanā-upekkhā).

Among those two types of equanimity, the equanimity regarding forms is of one kind, and the equanimity regarding sounds and so forth is of another kind. For the equanimity regarding forms does not occur regarding sounds and so forth. The equanimity regarding forms takes only form as its object...
189:
The equanimity that arises does not arise in respect of sounds and so forth. Indeed, equanimity regarding visible forms (rūpa) takes only visible forms as its object, not sounds and so forth. Regarding the nature of equanimity in visible forms, one type of tranquility-equanimity (samatha-upekkhā) arises by taking the earth-kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa) as its object, while another arises by taking the water-kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa) and so forth as its object. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to analyze diversity (nānatta) and that which is based on diversity (nānattasita), said: "Monks, there is equanimity regarding visible forms," and so on.

However, because there are not two or three [types of] the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) and so forth, the Blessed One, wishing to analyze unity (ekatta) and that which is based on unity (ekattasita), said: "Monks, there is equanimity based on the sphere of infinite space," and so on.

In that context, equanimity of the sphere of infinite space is based on the sphere of infinite space by way of association (sampayutta). For one who contemplates the aggregates of the sphere of infinite space with insight, insight-equanimity (vipassanā-upekkhā) is based on the sphere of infinite space by way of the object (ārammaṇa). The same method applies to the remaining terms such as "based on the sphere of infinite consciousness" (viññāṇañcāyatana-nissita).

In the passage "Abandon that equanimity," he causes the abandonment of equanimity associated with the fine-material sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti) by means of equanimity associated with the immaterial sphere attainments (arūpāvacara-samāpatti). He causes the abandonment of insight-equanimity that takes fine-material phenomena as its object by means of insight-equanimity that takes immaterial phenomena as its object.

In the term "atammayatā" (non-identification), "tammayatā" refers to craving (taṇhā). Because it leads to the exhaustion of that craving, insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) is called "atammayatā." "Abandon that equanimity" means that in this context, by means of insight leading to emergence, he causes the abandonment of both equanimity associated with immaterial sphere attainments and insight-equanimity.

"Yad-ariyo" refers to those foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) which the Noble One, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, frequents. In that regard, the Buddha, establishing mindfulness in three instances, should be understood as frequenting the foundations of mindfulness. "Na sussūsanti" means they do not wish to listen with faith. "Na aññā" means they do not apply their minds for the sake of knowledge. "Vokkammā" means having bypassed. "Satthu sāsanā" means they do not consider that the Teacher's instruction should be accepted or fulfilled. 

"Na ca attamano" means he is not [personally] delighted. Here, it should not be understood that he becomes displeased by way of household-based grief (gehasita-domanassa). Rather, this was said because there is no cause for delight in disciples who do not practice. "Anavassuto" means being without the flow of ill-will (paṭigha). "Sato sampajāno" means with mindfulness and with wisdom...
190:
...endowed with. "Upekkhako" means he is equanimous with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). "Attamano" (delighted): here too, it should not be understood as being elated by way of household-based joy (gehasita-somanassa). Rather, this was said because there is no cause for lack of delight in disciples who practice well. "Anavassuto" means being without the flow of lust (rāga).

"Sārito" means tamed or disciplined. "Runs in only one direction" means that if one runs without turning back, one can only run in one direction; but if one turns back, one can run in another direction. "Runs in eight directions" means that while sitting in a single cross-legged position, without turning the body, one can run in eight directions simultaneously by the power of the deliverances (vimokkha). Alternatively, it means that while sitting facing the east, or facing any other direction such as the south, one enters the eight attainments (samāpatti). The rest of the text is clear in all places.

## The Explanation of the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, named Papañcasūdanī, is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta. In that sutta, "Uddesavibhaṅga" means the summary (uddesa/mātikā) and the analysis (vibhaṅga/vibhajana). "Upaparikkhitabba" means it should be weighed, judged, investigated, and discerned. "Bahiddhā" means in external objects. "Avikkhittaṃ avisaṭaṃ" (unscattered, undiffused): being established in an object by way of attachment (nikanti) is called "scattered" or "diffused"; wishing to prohibit this, he spoke thus. "Ajjhattaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ" means not being fixed by way of attachment in one's internal sphere (gocarajjhatta). "Anupādāya na paritasserya" means one should not be attached to that consciousness without grasping or clinging through craving. It means that a monk should investigate in such a way that consciousness is not scattered or diffused among external objects, is not fixed internally by attachment, and does not crave through non-clinging. "Jātijarāmaraṇadukkhasamudayasambhavo" means there is no more arising of birth, aging, death, and the remaining mass of suffering.
191:
‘One who follows the sign of forms’ (rūpanimittānusārī) means one who follows or runs after forms, which are the causes of defilements, by way of longing and so forth. 

Friends, ‘not settled internally’ (ajjhattaṃ asanthitaṃ) means not being settled in objects such as the kasinas by way of lustful attachment. Indeed, not being settled in an object by way of lustful attachment does not lead to a state of decline; rather, it only leads to a state of distinction [such as the attainment of jhāna or the path]. 

‘Agitation without clinging’ (anupādā paritassanā): In the Khandhavagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Teacher taught, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you agitation with clinging (upādāparitassanā) and non-agitation without clinging (anupādāaparitassanā),” taking it in this way: if there is clinging, there is agitation; if there is no clinging, there is no agitation. Among these two, the Great Elder Mahākaccāna, wishing to show that even agitation with clinging is [in a sense] agitation without clinging, spoke in this way. How can this be agitation without clinging? It is because there is no object that is truly fit to be clung to. If any conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhāra) were permanent, stable, a self, or belonging to a self, and thus fit to be clung to, then this agitation would indeed be agitation with clinging. However, since there is no such conditioned phenomenon fit to be clung to, even when one clings to form as self and so forth, in reality, it remains unclung to. Therefore, it should be understood that although this agitation occurs by the power of wrong view as agitation with clinging, in its ultimate sense, it is indeed agitation without clinging.

‘Becomes otherwise’ (aññathā hoti) means it changes and perishes, giving up its natural state. ‘Following the change of form’ (rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattī) means that kamma-consciousness follows the destruction of form in such ways as, “My form has changed,” or “Alas, that which was, is no more for me.” ‘Born of following the change’ (vipariṇāmānuparivattaja) means born from the mind that takes the changing form as its object. ‘Agitation and the arising of [unwholesome] states’ (paritassanā dhammasamuppādā) means agitation due to craving and the arising of unwholesome states. ‘They remain having overwhelmed the mind’ (cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti) means they remain having exhausted, seized, and overwhelmed the wholesome mind. ‘Fearful’ (uttāsavā) means being with agitation due to dread as well as agitation due to craving. ‘Distressed’ (vighātavā) means being with distress and suffering. ‘Longing’ (apekkhavā) means being with attachment and affection. 

Friends, ‘thus there is agitation without clinging’ means that agitation occurs without clinging afterwards, like a person who, perceiving a box as containing a gem, takes hold of an empty box, and later falls into distress when that box is lost. ‘Not following the change of form’ (na ca rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattī) means that for an Arahant, the kamma-consciousness no longer follows the destruction of form. The remaining terms are clear in all their meanings.
192:
‘Not following the change of form’ means that for the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), kamma-consciousness itself no longer exists; therefore, there is no following the destruction of form. The rest is clear in every respect.

## The Commentary on the Uddesavibhanga Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, is finished.

## 9. Araṇavibhaṅgasutta-vaṇṇanā

“Thus have I heard” and so forth refers to the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, ‘should not extol and should not disparage’ (nevussādeyya na apasādeyya) means one should not lift up or put down any person by way of defilements based on the household life. ‘Should teach only the Dhamma’ means one should speak only of the true nature of things. ‘Determining happiness’ (sukhavinicchaya) means happiness that has been determined. ‘Speaking in private’ (raho vāda) means speaking of someone’s faults behind their back, which is malicious speech. ‘Should not disparage to one’s face’ (sammukhā na khīṇa) means one should not speak words that are very disparaging, confused, or defiled even to one’s face. ‘Should not speak with dogmatic clinging’ (nābhiniveseyya) means one should not speak by firmly grasping and holding [to views]. ‘Convention’ (samañña) refers to worldly designations and worldly concepts. ‘Should not overstep’ (nātidhāveyya) means one should not transgress.

‘One who has happiness connected to sensual pleasures’ (kāmapaṭisandhisukhino) refers to a person who has reached happiness through pleasure associated with the objects of sensuality and the defilements of sensuality. ‘Accompanied by suffering’ (sadukkho) means accompanied by suffering through the suffering of resultants (vipāka-dukkha) and the suffering of defilements (saṅkilesa-dukkha). ‘Accompanied by injury’ (saupaghāto) means accompanied by injury through the injury of resultants and the injury of defilements. The same applies to ‘accompanied by burning’ (sapariḷāho). ‘Wrong practice’ (micchāpaṭipadā) means an improper practice, an unwholesome practice.

‘Thus he disparages some’ (ittheke apasādeti) means he disparages certain persons in this way by way of defilements based on the household life. The same method applies to extolling. ‘Fetter to existence’ (bhavasaṃyojana) means the bond to existence, which is a name for craving.
