## 12. Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta. In that sutta, regarding the name "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī," "Gotamī" is the clan name. On the day of her naming, the Brahmins in attendance, seeing her possession of auspicious marks, prophesied: "If this princess has a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a Universal Monarch. If she has a son, he will become a Universal Monarch. Thus, in either case, her progeny (pajā) will be great." Therefore, they gave her the name "Mahāpajāpatī." In this sutta, however, she is referred to as "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī," combining it with her clan name. "Navaṃ" refers to something new that has not yet been soiled. "Sāmaṃ vāyitaṃ" (woven by herself) does not mean she wove it entirely with her own hands; rather, it refers to a day when, surrounded by a group of nurses, she went to the weavers' workshop, took hold of the end of the shuttle, and made the gesture of weaving. It is said in reference to that.

At what time did the thought of offering a pair of cloths to the Blessed One arise in Gotamī? It was when He first returned to Kapilavatthu after attaining Buddhahood. At that time, King Suddhodana invited the Blessed One, who had entered for alms, into his palace. Then, seeing the beauty of the Blessed One's physical form, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī thought, "How beautiful is my son's physical form!" and a powerful joy arose in her. Then she thought, "While my son lived at home for twenty-nine years, I never gave him even so much as a banana; now I will give him a set of robes." She further thought, "Although there are many costly cloths in this palace, they do not satisfy me. Only what is made by my own hands will satisfy me. Therefore, I will make it with my own hands and offer it."
220:
After thinking thus, she had cotton brought from the market, and by her own hands, she performed the tasks of ginning and carding, and then spun fine thread. She had a weaving shed built within the palace grounds, summoned weavers, and had them weave the cloth, providing them with the same fine food and snacks that she herself consumed. From time to time, surrounded by a group of nurses, she would go and hold the end of the loom to assist. When the weaving was finished, she gave great rewards to the weavers, placed the pair of cloths in a perfumed casket to let the fragrance permeate, and thinking, "I will take these robes for my son (Prince Siddhattha)," she informed King Suddhodana. The King had the road to the Nigrodhārāma monastery prepared. He ordered the streets to be swept, water-pots to be placed, and banners and flags to be raised, arranging the path from the royal palace to the Nigrodhārāma and sprinkling it with flowers. Mahāpajāpatī, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by nurses, carried the casket on her head, went to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, this is a new pair of cloths of mine," and so forth.

"Dutiyaṃ pi kho" (For a second time) means—when the Buddha said, "Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha," she invited and pleaded, saying, "Venerable Sir, I am able to give robes to a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand monks from the cloth storehouse. However, this cloth was spun and woven by my own hands specifically for the Blessed One. Therefore, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One please accept it." Although she pleaded in this way up to three times, the Blessed One continued to refuse.

Why did the Blessed One have the robes that were being given to him offered to the Saṅgha? It was out of compassion for his aunt. This thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Because of me, three types of volitions—preliminary volition (pubba-cetanā), actual volition (muñca-cetanā), and subsequent volition (para-cetanā)—have arisen in my aunt. Let these volitions also arise in her because of the Saṅgha. In this way, her six volitions will combine and lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time." However, a Vitaṇḍavādī (sophist) says, "It was said so because giving to the Saṅgha is of great fruit." That person should be asked: "Do you say that giving to the Saṅgha is more fruitful than giving to the Teacher?" If he says, "Yes, I say so," then tell him, "Bring forth a Sutta passage." The Vitaṇḍavādī brings forth the passage: "Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored, and the Saṅgha will be honored too." When asked, "Is this the only meaning of this Sutta?" he admits, "Yes, that is all." If that were the case, then according to the statements, "Ānanda, give the cake to the scavengers (vighāsāda)," and "Kaccāna, give the molasses to the scavengers," giving to scavengers would also be especially fruitful. This is also true: the Blessed One often has things given to him bestowed upon others. Therefore, you (the Vitaṇḍavādī) should not hold such a view. Kings and great ministers often have the gifts brought to them given to elephant trainers and others. Are those elephant trainers superior to the kings? Therefore, do not hold such a view. Because it is taught, "In this world or the next, there is no one superior or equal to the Buddha; he has reached the pinnacle of those worthy of offerings and gives great fruit to those desiring merit," there is no individual worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) superior to the Buddha.
221:
Regarding the statement, 'He causes what is offered to him to be given to others,' kings, great ministers, and the like also cause the gifts brought to them to be given to elephant keepers, cowherds, and so on. Do those elephant keepers and others then become superior to the kings and such? Therefore, do not hold the view [that the recipient is more noble].

'Neither in this world nor in the world beyond,
Does there exist one superior to or equal to the Buddha;
He has reached the pinnacle of those worthy of offerings,
For those seeking merit and searching for vast fruits.'

Because of this teaching, there is no recipient of offerings more excellent or superior to the Teacher. Intending that the six-fold volition of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī would thus become unified and lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time, the Buddha refused her three times and caused her to give it to the Saṅgha.

He also spoke thus to inspire respect for the Saṅgha in future generations. It occurred to the Buddha: 'I will not remain for long, but my Sāsana will be established in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha; let future generations develop respect for the Saṅgha.' Thus, he refused three times and caused her to give it to the Saṅgha. If this is so, future generations will think, 'The Teacher caused even what was offered to himself to be given to the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha is indeed a worthy recipient of offerings.' Having developed respect for the Saṅgha, they will consider it proper to offer the four requisites. The Saṅgha, without being weary for the four requisites, will learn the Word of the Buddha and practice the Dhamma of a recluse. In this way, my Sāsana will endure for five thousand years. From the request, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept [the offering],' it should also be understood that there is no recipient of offerings superior to the Teacher. Indeed, the Elder Ānanda had no grudge or enmity toward Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Nor did the Elder wish that her offering should not be of great fruit. The Elder, being wise, learned, and having attained the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) of a trainee (sekha), clearly saw the great fruit of an offering given to the Teacher and thus pleaded for him to accept it, saying, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept it.'

Furthermore, a Vitandavādī (sophist) says: 'Because of the statement, "If it is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored and the Saṅgha too," is the Teacher not included within the Saṅgha?' That person should be asked: 'Do you know how many refuges there are, and how many kinds of unshakeable faith (aveccappasāda) there are?' If he knows, he will say 'three.' Then he should be told: 'According to your doctrine, since the Teacher is included in the Saṅgha, there would be only two.' If that were the case, [the passage] 'Monks, I allow the going forth and the higher ordination by these three refuges...' (Mahāvagga, 34).
222:
'I allow the going forth and the higher ordination by these three refuges' (Mahāvagga, 34)—under the Vitandavādī's view, neither this going forth nor this higher ordination would be valid. If that were so, you would be neither a monk nor a layman. Furthermore, while the Fully Enlightened One is residing in the Gandhakuṭī, the monks perform the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and other legal acts of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma). If the Teacher were included in the Saṅgha, those acts would be invalid [due to his absence from the assembly], but they are not. Therefore, it should not be said that 'the Teacher is included in the Saṅgha.'

'Āpādikā' means one who makes one grow (a nurturer). It means one who cared for and made your hands and feet grow when they could not yet perform their functions. 'Posikā' means one who reared you by bathing, feeding, and giving you drink two or three times a day. 'She gave milk' refers to the fact that Prince Nanda was reportedly only a few days younger than the Bodhisatta. When that prince was born, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī gave her own son to nurses and, performing the duties of a nurse for the Bodhisatta herself, she gave him her own milk. Referring to this, the Elder Ānanda spoke thus. Having thus spoken of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī's great helpfulness, the Blessed One, now wishing to show his own great helpfulness, said 'Bhagavāpi, bhante,' and so on. There, 'Bhagavantaṃ, bhante, āgamma' means because of, depending on, or in reference to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to express his appreciation (anumodanā) even more regarding the two kinds of help, said 'Evametaṃ,' and so on. There, 'Ānanda, depending on which person' means a resident pupil (antevāsika) depending on a teacher. 'Ānanda, for this person by this person' means I say it is not easy for this resident pupil to make a return of help to this teacher. Among 'Abhivādana' and so on, 'Abhivādana' means performing an act of respect upon seeing the teacher. Or, it is bowing while facing the direction where the teacher resides, whether while going, sitting, or lying down. Rising from one's seat to greet the teacher upon seeing him from afar is called 'Paccuṭṭhāna.' Seeing the teacher and raising the joined palms to the head to pay homage, or doing the same while facing his direction whether walking, standing, or sitting, is called 'Añjalikamma.' Performing suitable duties is called 'Sāmīcikamma.' Regarding robes and so on, when offering a robe, one does not offer just any robe, but offers a costly robe worth a hundred, five hundred, or a thousand [pieces of currency]. The same should be understood for almsfood and other requisites.
223:
It is indeed a gift. The same method should be understood regarding alms-food and so forth. What more is there to say? Even if one were to fill the entire universe with the four excellent requisites, using Mount Sineru as the pinnacle, and offer it, one would still not be able to adequately repay the debt of gratitude to one's teacher.

Why did He begin the discourse with the words 'Cuddasa kho panimā' and so forth? This sutta arose concerning offerings made to specific individuals (pāṭipuggalika dakkhiṇā). The Elder Ānanda also encouraged the making of an individual offering, saying, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept it.' He began this teaching to show that an offering made in fourteen instances is called an individual offering (pāṭipuggalika).

'Ayaṃ paṭhamā' means this offering is the first in terms of virtue and in terms of excellence. This offering alone is the first, the foremost, and the greatest; there is no measure to this offering. The second and third offerings are also supreme offerings. The remaining offerings do not reach the state of being supreme offerings.

'Bāhirake kāmesu vītarāge' refers to those outside the Dispensation who are free from sensual lust, who hold the doctrines of kamma and action (kammavādī and kiriyavādī), and who possess the five mundane superknowledges (lokiya-pañcābhiññā).

'Puthujjana-sīlavante' means a virtuous worldling is one who is gentle by nature like a cow, without deceit or hypocrisy, and who makes a living righteously and fairly through farming or trade without harming others.

'Puthujjana-dussīle' means immoral worldlings are those like fishermen and fish-trappers who make a living by harming others.

Now, wishing to define the fruit of an individual offering, He said 'Tatra Ānanda' and so forth. In that context, 'tiracchānagate' (regarding animals) does not refer to giving for the purpose of nurturing out of appreciation for their qualities or help. Nor does it refer to giving just a morsel or half a morsel of food. It refers to giving as much as desired to any animal that happens to arrive—such as a dog, pig, chicken, or crow—expecting a result, and it is with this intention that He said, 'having given a gift to an animal.'

'Sataguṇā' means having a hundredfold blessing. 'Paṭikaṅkhitabbā' means should be desired. This is what is meant: this offering gives five hundred blessings, namely: a hundredfold life-span, a hundredfold beauty, a hundredfold happiness, a hundredfold strength, and a hundredfold wisdom. It gives life, beauty, happiness, strength, and wisdom in a hundred existences, and it produces these results without remainder. Even when 'a hundred births' is said, this is the same meaning. In this way, the method should be applied in all cases.

'Sotāpattiphala-sacchikiriyāya paṭipanne': in this phrase, at the lowest level, even a lay devotee (upāsaka) who has gone to the three refuges is called one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. An offering given to such a person has incalculable and immeasurable fruit. An offering given to one established in the five precepts has greater fruit than an offering given to that practicing person. An offering given to one established in the ten precepts has greater fruit than an offering given to one established in the five precepts. An offering given to a novice (sāmaṇera) ordained on that very day...
224:
Greater in fruit than that (offering to one established in the five precepts) is an offering to one established in the ten precepts. Greater than that is an offering to a novice (sāmaṇera) ordained on that very day. Greater than that is an offering to an ordained monk (upasampanna-bhikkhu). Greater than that is an offering to an ordained monk who is perfect in his duties (vattasampanna). Greater than that is an offering to one practicing insight (vipassaka). Greater than that is an offering to one who has begun insight (āraddhavipassaka). At the highest level, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is the person endowed with the path (maggasamaṅgī). An offering given to such a person is even greater in fruit than those mentioned before.

If it is asked, 'Is it possible to give an offering to one endowed with the path?' the answer is, 'Yes, it is possible.' For when a monk who has begun insight takes his bowl and robes and enters the village for alms, people take the bowl from the hand of that monk standing at the door of the house and pour in food and snacks. If at that moment the monk emerges from the path (attains the path), this offering is called one given to a person endowed with the path. Or else, he might be seated in the refectory, and people go and place food and snacks in his bowl. If at that moment he emerges from the path, this offering is also called one given to a person endowed with the path. Or else, while he is seated in the monastery or the refectory, lay devotees take his bowl, go to their own houses, and pour in food and snacks. If at that moment he emerges from the path, this offering is also called one given to a person endowed with the path. In that case, the incalculability of the offering given to one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry should be understood like the water in a pond. But the superior incalculability of an offering given to a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and so forth should be understood like the water in the five great rivers and the great ocean. This meaning can also be illustrated by the immeasurable quantity of dust, starting from the dust in a place the size of a threshing floor on the ground up to the dust of the great earth.

Why did He begin the discourse with 'Satta kho panimā' and so forth? Because it was said, 'Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha; when a gift is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored and the Saṅgha will be honored too.' He began this teaching to show that an offering given in seven instances is called an offering given to the Saṅgha. Among those seven, 'buddhappamukha ubhatosaṅgha' means the Saṅgha of monks on one side and the Saṅgha of nuns on the other, with the Teacher seated in the middle. This is the first offering. There is no offering equal in measure to this offering. The second offering and so forth do not reach the level of this supreme offering.
225:
Is it possible to give an offering to the dual Saṅgha headed by the Buddha after the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna? It is possible. How is it possible? One should place an image containing relics in a seat in front of the dual Saṅgha, set up a support, and starting with the libation water, first offer all the gift-objects to the Blessed One, and then give to the dual Saṅgha. By giving in this way, it is called an offering given to the dual Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. In that case, what should be done with the items offered to the Blessed One? They should be given to a monk who is accomplished in duties and who attends to the Blessed One. Just as a father's property goes to the son, it is also proper to give it to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Furthermore, taking the ghee and oil, lamps should be lit; taking the cloth, banners should be raised. 

'In the Bhikkhu Saṅgha' means the unlimited great Bhikkhu Saṅgha. The same method should be understood for the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. 'Gotrabhū' means those who enjoy only the lineage, monks in name only. 'Kāsāvakaṇṭha' refers to those known as 'yellow-necks.' It is said that they will wander about with a fragment of a yellow robe tied to their hand or neck. Their household life, wives and children, and work such as farming and trading will be just like those of ordinary people. In the phrase 'they will give offerings to the Saṅgha directed towards those immoral ones,' it is not said 'to the immoral Saṅgha.' This is because there is no such thing as an immoral Saṅgha. Immoral lay followers, however, give offerings directed towards the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, saying, 'We give to the Saṅgha,' while giving to those immoral monks. 

Thus, the Blessed One said that an offering given to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is immeasurable in terms of its benefits. Even an offering given to the Kāsāvakaṇṭha Saṅgha is said to be immeasurable in terms of its benefits. Indeed, an offering made to the Saṅgha belongs to one who is able to show respect toward the Saṅgha. However, showing respect toward the Saṅgha is very difficult. 

If someone, intending to give an offering to the Saṅgha, prepares the gift-objects, goes to the monastery, and says, 'Venerable sirs, please provide an elder on behalf of the Saṅgha,' but then, upon receiving a novice from the Saṅgha, becomes disappointed, thinking, 'I have received a novice,' his offering is not one made to the Saṅgha. Even if he receives a great elder and feels joy, thinking, 'I have received a great elder,' it is still not a Saṅghika-dāna. But if someone receives any person from the Saṅgha—whether a novice, an ordained monk, a young monk, an elder, an ignorant monk, or a wise monk—and without any doubt or discrimination, is able to show respect toward the Saṅgha, thinking, 'I give to the Saṅgha,' then his offering is truly one made to the Saṅgha. It is said that those living on the other side of the ocean act in this way.
226:
In that dispensation, a certain householder who was a monastery donor, thinking, 'I will give an offering directed to the Saṅgha,' requested from the Saṅgha, 'Please grant me one monk.' Although he received an immoral monk, he had the place where the monk would sit cleaned, prepared a seat, hung a canopy above, honored him with scents, incense, and flowers, washed his feet, anointed them with oil, and gave the gift-objects with a heart of respect for the Saṅgha, as if showing reverence to the Buddha. Later, after the meal, when that monk came to the door of the house and said, 'Give me a hoe for cleaning the monastery,' the lay follower, while still sitting, kicked the hoe toward him with his foot and said, 'Take it.' Then people said to him, 'You could not stop talking about the respect you showed this monk early this morning, but now there is not even a trace of proper conduct. What kind of behavior is this?' The lay follower replied, 'Sirs, that respect was for the Saṅgha, not for this individual.' 

If it is asked, 'Who purifies the offering given to the Kāsāvakaṇṭha Saṅgha?' the eighty great elders, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, purify it. Furthermore, although those elders have long since attained Parinibbāna, the Arahants who are still living today, starting from those elders, continue to purify that offering. 

'Ananda, I do not say that an offering to the Saṅgha is in any way (inferior to an individual offering)'—in this statement, there is the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, the Saṅgha of the present, and the Kāsāvakaṇṭha Saṅgha of the future. The Saṅgha headed by the Buddha should not be compared with the Saṅgha of the present, and the Saṅgha of the present should not be compared with the Kāsāvakaṇṭha Saṅgha of the future. Each should be spoken of according to its own time. A worldling monk received on behalf of the Saṅgha is superior to a Sotāpanna who is given to as an individual. For one who is able to show respect toward the Saṅgha, giving to a worldling monk is of greater fruit. The same method applies to the cases where a Sotāpanna received on behalf of the Saṅgha is superior to a Sakadāgāmī given to as an individual, and so on. For one who is able to show respect toward the Saṅgha, an offering given to an immoral person received on behalf of the Saṅgha is of greater fruit than an offering given to an Arahant as an individual. 

As for the statement, 'Great King, a gift given to a virtuous person is of great fruit, but not so one given to an immoral person,' that should be understood by setting aside this method and looking at the fourfold 'Purification of Offerings' (Dakkhiṇā-visuddhi), where it says, 'Ananda, there are these four purifications of offerings.' 

'Purified by the giver' means it is purified by being of great fruit; it means it becomes of great fruit. 'Kalyāṇa-dhamma' means having a pure nature, not an evil nature. In this context of 'purified by the giver,' King Vessantara should be mentioned. He gave his children to the Brahmin Jūjaka and caused the earth to tremble.
227:
"Purified by the recipient": In this context, the story of the fisherman living at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River should be told. It is said that this fisherman had given alms-food to the Elder Dīghasoma three times. While lying on his deathbed, he said, "The alms-food given to the Venerable Elder Dīghasoma rescues me [from the lower realms]."

"Purified by neither the giver [nor the recipient]": In this context, the story of the hunter living in Vaḍḍhamāna should be told. That hunter, intending to give an offering for his deceased parents, gave to an immoral monk three times. On the third time, the parent who had become a peta (hungry ghost) cried out, "An immoral person is robbing me!" However, when he gave to a virtuous monk and shared the merit, the benefit reached them.

"Purified by both the giver and the recipient": In this context, the Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa-dāna) should be told.

"That offering is purified by the giver": In this context, just as a skilled farmer, even if he obtains poor soil, plows it at the right time, removes the dust, plants good seeds, and guards it day and night without negligence, obtains more grain than another person's fertile field [that is poorly managed]; likewise, a virtuous person, even when giving to an immoral person, attains great fruit. In this manner, purification in all cases should be understood.

"One free from lust gives to those free from lust": In this context, "one free from lust" refers to a Non-returner (Anāgāmī). An Arahant, however, is one who is absolutely free from lust. Therefore, an offering given by an Arahant to an Arahant is indeed supreme. Why? Because there is no attachment to existence or longing for existence. If it is asked, "Does an Arahant not believe in the fruit of giving?" [The answer is:] Those who believe in the fruit of giving are not like Arahants. The action performed by an Arahant, being free from desire and lust, does not become wholesome (kusala) or unwholesome (akusala), but remains at the level of functional (kiriya). Therefore, they say that the Arahant's gift is supreme.

Is the gift given by the Blessed One to the Elder Sāriputta of great fruit, or is the gift given by the Elder Sāriputta to the Blessed One of great fruit? They say that the gift given by the Blessed One to the Elder Sāriputta is of great fruit. For, except for the Blessed One, there is no one else capable of knowing the result of a gift. To one who can give a gift with the four accomplishments (sampadā), it yields results in that very life. Herein, these are the accomplishments: the gift (deyyadhamma) is righteously obtained, the three stages of volition (cetanā) are intense, the recipient is an Arahant endowed with special qualities, and the recipient has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) on that very day.

The Dakkhiṇavibhaṅga Sutta is finished. The Vibhaṅgavāra is finished.

## 5. Saḷāyatanavagga, 1. Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta.

"Thus have I heard" and so forth; this is the Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta. In that sutta, "severely ill" means being on one's deathbed due to intense pain. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika, throughout his life, used to visit the Buddha regularly once, twice, or three times a day. Just as much as he visited the Buddha, he also served and attended to the senior Elders.
228:
Obtaining the gift righteously and fairly without oppressing others, the greatness of volition through the power of preliminary volition and so forth, the excellence of qualities due to being an Arahant, and being endowed with the accomplishment of the object (vatthu-sampadā) due to emerging from the attainment of cessation on that day.

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Fourth Vagga is finished.
229:
## 5. Saḷāyatanavagga
## 1. Explanation of the Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta. Therein, "bāḷhagilāno" means being extremely ill and having reached the deathbed. "Āmantesi"—it is heard that as long as the householder Anāthapiṇḍika could walk, he attended upon the Buddha without fail once, twice, or three times a day. Just as much as he attended upon the Teacher, he also served the Great Elders. Today, because his ability to walk was cut off and he had reached the bed from which he could not rise, wishing to send a message, he called a certain man and spoke. "Tenupasaṅkami" means that (Venerable Sāriputta), having asked permission from the Blessed One, approached at the time of sunset.

"Paṭikkamanti" means they recede, they become sparse. "Abhikkamanti" means they increase, they overwhelm, they become strong.

"Abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamo" means that when the pain ending in death arises, it is like a fire burning upwind. As long as the kamma-born heat (kammaja-tejo) is not exhausted, even with great effort, it is impossible to calm that painful feeling; only when the kamma-born heat is exhausted does it subside.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta thought: "The pain of this great merchant ends in death; it cannot be averted. Other talk is useless; I will preach a Dhamma discourse to this merchant." Then, wishing to preach that discourse to him, he said the words beginning with "Tasmātiha." Therein, "tasmā" means because one who grasps the eye with the three kinds of grasping—craving, conceit, and wrong view—is unable to avert the arisen pain ending in death, therefore (it is said). "Na cakkhuṃ upādiyissāmi" means "I will not grasp the eye with the three kinds of grasping." "Na ca me cakkhunissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ" means "My eye-consciousness will also not arise depending on the eye-sensitivity." In the words "na rūpaṃ," the form as an object (rūpāyatana) was preached below; here, however, he speaks referring to all forms included in the sense sphere (kāma-bhava).

"Na idhalokaṃ" means "I will not grasp either the place of residence or food and clothing." This was preached for the purpose of not being attached to the four requisites. "Na..."
230:
In this context, the word "paraloka" (the world beyond) refers to all worlds except the human world. This was spoken to abandon the kind of craving such as, "Having been reborn in such and such a heaven, I will be in such and such a place; I will eat this, enjoy this, wear this, and clothe myself in this." The Elder concluded the teaching by reaching the peak of Arahantship, freeing [the householder] from the three types of grasping, thinking, "I will not cling to that world beyond, nor will my consciousness be dependent on it."

"Olīyasi" means being bound to or clinging to sense objects upon seeing one's own prosperity. Thinking, "If even a householder as faithful and devoted as Anāthapiṇḍika is afraid of the danger of death, who else would not be afraid?" the Venerable Ānanda, wishing to give firm advice to the householder, spoke thus. When the lay follower said, "I have never heard such a Dhamma talk before," he meant, "I have never heard such a Dhamma talk even from the Blessed One." Does the Blessed One not give such subtle and profound talks? It is not that He does not. However, this householder had never before heard a talk that incorporates the six internal bases, the six external bases, the six classes of consciousness, the six classes of contact, the six classes of feeling, the six elements, the five aggregates, the four formless states, this world, and the world beyond, and then directs them towards Arahantship through the power of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. That is why he spoke thus.

Furthermore, this lay follower was one who was deeply inclined toward and delighted in giving (dāna). Whenever he went to the presence of the Buddhas, he never went empty-handed. If he went in the morning, he would have gruel, food, and so on brought along. If he went in the afternoon, he would have ghee, honey, molasses, and so on brought along. If those were not available, he would have sand brought and scattered in the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī). Only after giving and observing the precepts would he return home. It is said that this lay follower followed the practice of Bodhisattas. Therefore, for twenty-four years, the Blessed One mostly gave him talks on giving (dānakathā), saying, "Lay follower, this giving is the path traveled by the Bodhisattas; it is also the path traveled by me. I have practiced giving for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. You are merely following the path I have traveled." The Great Disciples, such as the Marshal of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), also used to give him talks on giving whenever he came to them. That is why Venerable Ānanda said, "Householder, such a Dhamma talk does not occur to white-clad laypeople." The meaning is: Householder, laypeople have intense longing and intense...
231:
...obsession with craving for fields, lands, silver, gold, female slaves, male slaves, children, wives, and so on. To them, the talk "One should not have longing for these things, one should not have craving for them" does not occur and is not pleasing.

"Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami" (approached where the Blessed One was): Why did he approach? It is said that as soon as he was reborn in the Tusita heaven, seeing his own physical form shining like a great mass of gold three gāvutas in height, and seeing his prosperity such as gardens and celestial mansions, he reflected, "This prosperity of mine is indeed great. What good deed did I perform in the human world?" Seeing his extraordinary merit toward the Triple Gem, he thought, "This state of being a deity is a place of negligence. If I delight in this prosperity, I might lose mindfulness. Let me go now and speak in praise of my Jetavana monastery, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Noble Path, and the Elder Sāriputta, and only after returning from there will I enjoy this prosperity." He did exactly that. To show this, the words beginning with "Atha kho Anāthapiṇḍiko" were spoken.

Therein, "isisaṅghanisevitaṃ" means the Jetavana monastery frequented by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Having praised the Jetavana with the first verse in this way, he now spoke the words beginning with "kammaṃ vijjā ca" to praise the Noble Path. Therein, "kamma" (action) refers to the volition (cetanā) associated with the Path. "Vijjā" (knowledge) refers to the wisdom (paññā) of the Path. "Dhamma" refers to the states belonging to the side of concentration (samādhi). "Sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamaṃ" (virtue is the best life) shows that the life of one established in virtue is supreme. Alternatively, "vijjā" refers to Right View and Right Intention; "dhamma" refers to Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration; "sīla" refers to Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood. The life of one established in this virtue is supreme. By this eightfold path, beings are purified.

"Tasmā" (therefore) is said because beings are purified only by the Path, not by lineage or wealth. "Yoniso vicine dhammaṃ" means one should investigate the states associated with concentration with wise means; thus one is purified in that Noble Path. Alternatively, one should investigate the five aggregates with wise means; thus one is purified in those Four Noble Truths.

Now, to praise the qualities of the Elder Sāriputta, he spoke the words beginning with "Sāriputto va." Therein, "Sāriputto va" is an emphatic statement, meaning that Sāriputta alone is supreme by way of this wisdom and so on. "Upasamena" means by the calming of defilements.
232:
"Pārangato" means one who has reached Nibbāna. Any monk who has reached Nibbāna should be considered as having reached the highest limit; it means there is no elder who is superior to the Elder Sāriputta. The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all respects.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī
## The Explanation of the Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Channovāda Sutta
The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Channovāda Sutta. In that sutta, "Channa" refers to the elder of this name; he is not the Minister Channa (Elder Channa) who accompanied [the Bodhisatta] during the Great Renunciation. "Paṭisallāna" refers to emerging from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Gilānapucchaka" (inquirer of the sick) is said because the Blessed One praised attending to the sick. "Sattha" refers to a weapon that takes life. "Nāvakankhāmi" means "I do not desire."

"Anupavajja" refers to the state of not arising again, of not having relinking (rebirth).

The words beginning with "Etaṃ mama" (This is mine) are spoken by way of grasping through craving, conceit, and views (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi). "Seeing cessation" (nirodhaṃ disvā) means knowing the exhaustion and passing away (khaya-vaya). "I see that 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'" means seeing as impermanence, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta).

"Tasmā" (Therefore) is said because, being unable to endure the pains ending in death, he said, "I will take the weapon." Since the Venerable Channa was a worldling (puthujjana), this was pointed out to mean "reflect on this word as well." "Niccakappa" means at all times. "Nissitassa" (for one who is dependent) refers to a worldling who is attached by craving and views. "Calita" means trembling or agitation. "Passaddhi" means the tranquility of body and mind, the tranquility from defilements.

"Nati" means the inclination of craving. "Natiyā asati" (when there is no inclination) means the absence of longing for new existence, delight, and the obsession of defilements. "There is no coming or going" (āgatigati na hoti) means there is no coming by way of rebirth and no going by way of death. "Cutūpapāta" means death and rebirth. "Neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two" means it does not occur anywhere. This itself is the end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) and the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha). This is...
233:
...the definition, the state of being pure all around. Indeed, in this passage "Esevanto dukkhassa," this is the meaning: not occurring in this world or the next. As for those teachers who, taking the phrase "na ubhayamantarena," desire an intermediate existence (antarābhava), the answer to them has already been stated below.

"Sattham āharesi" means he took a life-taking weapon and cut his throat. Then, at that moment, the fear of death overcame the Elder Channa, and the sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) appeared. Realizing his status as a worldling, the elder felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega), established insight (vipassanā), and while discerning formations (saṅkhāra), he reached Arahantship and attained Parinibbāna as a "Samasīsī" (one who attains the end of defilements and life simultaneously). "The blamelessness was declared even in his presence" (sammukhāyeva anupavajjatā vyākatā) means that although this declaration was made while the elder was still a worldling, because of this declaration, his Parinibbāna occurred without obstacle. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke based on that very declaration. "Upavajjakulāni" refers to the families of supporters who should be visited. By this, the elder [Sāriputta] asked, "Venerable Sir, while such male and female lay supporters exist, will that monk attain Parinibbāna in your Dispensation?" Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the elder's lack of entanglement with families, said "Honti hete Sāriputta," etc. In this place, the Elder's state of being unentangled with families became evident. The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all places.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, Papañcasūdanī
## The Explanation of the Channovāda Sutta is finished.
## 3. Explanation of the Puṇṇovāda Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the beginning of the Puṇṇovāda Sutta. In that sutta, "paṭisallāna" means solitude. "Taṃ ca" refers to that eye and that visible form. "Nandīsamudayā dukkhasamudayo" means that due to the gathering of craving which delights (nandī-taṇhā), there is the simultaneous arising of the suffering of the five aggregates. Thus, at the six doors, by way of the two truths—the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin—He showed the truth pertaining to the round (vaṭṭa), bringing it to its climax. In the second method, "nirodho maggo" means that by way of the two truths—the truth of cessation and the truth of the path—He showed the truth of the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), bringing it to its climax. The connection "Iminā ca tvaṃ Puṇṇa" is a separate connection. Thus, having first included the teaching in Arahantship by way of the round and its cessation, He now said "Iminā ca tvaṃ," etc., wishing to make the Elder Puṇṇa roar his lion's roar in seven places.
234:
"Caṇḍa" refers to those who are corrupt and wicked. "Pharusa" refers to those who are harsh. "Will abuse" means they will abuse with the ten grounds of abuse. "Will threaten" means they will threaten by saying, "What kind of monk are you? We will do this and that to you." "In this way, in this place" means "In this reflection, it will be like this for me."

"With a stick" means with a four-cubit stick or a club (referring to beating). "With a weapon" means with a single-edged weapon and so on (referring to cutting). "They seek a weapon that takes life" means they search for a weapon that can take away life. The Elder said this in reference to the monks in the Third Pārājika case who, upon hearing the talk on foulness (asubha-kathā), became disgusted with their bodies and sought a weapon to take their own lives. In the term "damūpasamena," the name "dama" refers to the restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara) and so on. In the passage, "Tamed by truth, endowed with dama (restraint), reaching the end of the path, having lived the holy life," "dama" is said to be the restraint of the senses. In the passage, "If there is a quality greater than truth, dama, generosity, and patience in this world," "dama" is said to be wisdom (paññā). In the passage, "Through giving, dama, restraint, and truthful speech," "dama" is said to be the observance of the Uposatha. In this sutta, however, "dama" should be understood as patience (khanti). "Upasama" is simply a synonym for that "dama."

Regarding the words "Then the Venerable Puṇṇa," who is this Elder Puṇṇa, and why did he wish to go there? This Elder was a resident of the Sunāparanta region. Having noticed that living in Sāvatthī was not conducive to his practice, he wished to go to that Sunāparanta region.

The sequential account of that journey is as follows: It is said that there were two brothers in a merchant village in the Sunāparanta country. Among those brothers, the elder would sometimes take five hundred carts to the countryside to bring back goods; sometimes the younger brother would go. At this time, leaving the younger brother at home, the elder brother traveled through the countryside with five hundred carts and eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. He made camp not far from Jetavana Monastery, and after having his morning meal, he sat in a suitable place surrounded by his attendants.

At that time, the residents of Sāvatthī, having finished their morning meal, undertook the Uposatha precepts, donned clean upper robes, and carrying incense and flowers, set out from the south gate with minds inclined, leaned, and directed toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha...
235:
(The people) were going to Jetavana Monastery. The great merchant Puṇṇa saw them and asked a man, "Where are these people going?" The man replied, "Sir, do you not know? The Buddha-gem, the Dhamma-gem, and the Saṅgha-gem have appeared in the world. This great crowd is going to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One." For that Great Puṇṇa, the word "Buddha" pierced through his skin and so on, reaching and remaining in his bone marrow.

Then, surrounded by his attendants, he went to the monastery with that crowd. While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice, he stood at the edge of the assembly and, having heard the Dhamma, the desire to ordain arose in him. Then, the Blessed One, knowing the right time, dismissed the assembly. Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and invited Him for the next day. On the second day, he had a pavilion built, arranged seats, and offered a great gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. After his morning meal, he undertook the Uposatha precepts, called his treasurer, and said, "This much merchandise has been sold, and this much has not yet been sold," explaining everything. He handed over everything, saying, "Give this wealth to my younger brother." He then ordained in the presence of the Blessed One and became devoted to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

However, while he was reflecting on the meditation subject, it did not become clear to him. Therefore, he thought, "This region is not suitable for me (to develop meditation). It would be good if I take a meditation subject from the Blessed One and go back to my own place." Later, after wandering for alms in the morning and rising from seclusion in the evening, he approached the Blessed One, requested a meditation teaching, and after making seven bold "lion's roar" (sīhanāda) statements, he departed. Therefore, it is said, "Then the Venerable Puṇṇa... dwelt."

Where did this Elder dwell? He dwelt in four places. First, entering the Sunāparanta country and going to Ajjuhatta Mountain, he entered the merchant village for alms. Then his younger brother recognized him, offered almsfood, and made him promise, "Venerable Sir, do not go elsewhere; please stay right here," and made him dwell in that very place.

From there, he went to the monastery named Samuddagiri Vihāra. In that monastery, there was a walkway (caṅkama) demarcated with magnetite stones; no one was able to walk on that walkway. There, the ocean waves would come and strike the magnetite stones, making a great noise. The Elder, reflecting, "May it be a comfortable dwelling for the monks who are contemplating their meditation subjects," made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for the ocean to be silent.
236:
From there, he proceeded to the mountain named Mātulagiri. In that place, there were so many flocks of birds that their sounds were continuous day and night. The Elder reflected, "This place is not conducive to mental cultivation," and from there he went to the monastery named Makulakārāma. That monastery was neither too far from nor too near to the village of Vāṇijagāma, convenient for coming and going, secluded, and quiet. The Elder reflected, "This place is suitable for living in comfort," and having had places for the night, places for the day, and walkways (caṅkama) constructed at that Makulakārāma monastery, he entered the rains retreat. Thus, he resided in four places.

During that very rains retreat, one day, five hundred merchants planned, "We shall go to the other side of the ocean," and loaded their goods onto a ship. On the day of boarding the ship, the Elder's younger brother fed the Elder, took the precepts in the Elder's presence, and while departing after paying homage, said, "Venerable Sir, the great ocean is immeasurable and full of many dangers; please look after (protect) us," and then boarded the ship. As the ship traveled with great speed, it reached a certain small island. The people landed on the island, thinking, "We shall eat our morning meal." On that island, there were no other trees, only a sandalwood forest.

Then, one man struck a tree with a hatchet and, realizing it was red sandalwood, said, "Friends, we are traveling to the other side of the ocean for the sake of profit. There is no profit greater than this sandalwood. Even a small piece four finger-breadths long is worth a hundred thousand pieces of money. Therefore, let us discard the goods that should be discarded and fill the ship only with sandalwood." They did accordingly. The non-human beings (spirits) dwelling in the sandalwood forest became angry and thought, "These people have destroyed our sandalwood forest; let us kill them." Then they thought, "If we kill them on this island, the whole forest will smell of corpses. We will sink their ship in the middle of the ocean."

Then, a moment after they had boarded the ship and departed, the spirits stirred up waves and themselves displayed terrifying forms. The people were frightened and paid homage to their respective deities. The younger brother of the Elder, the householder Cūḷapuṇṇa, stood paying homage to the Elder, thinking, "May my brother, the Elder Puṇṇa, be my refuge."

At that very moment, the Elder, having reflected and known their impending disaster, flew through the air and stood at the prow of the ship. When the spirits saw the Elder, they said, "The Venerable Elder Puṇṇa has come," and fled; the waves also became calm. The Elder said, "Do not be afraid," and having comforted them, asked, "Where do you wish to go?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we wish to go only to our own place, the country of Sunāparanta." The Elder, stepping on a plank of the ship, made a determination: "Let this ship go to the place these people desire." The merchants reached their own place, Sunāparanta, and after telling their wives and children about the matter, said, "Come, let us go to pay respects to the Venerable Mahā Puṇṇa." The five hundred merchants, together with their five hundred wives, established themselves in the Three Refuges and requested to be lay followers. Then, unloading the goods from the ship, they informed the Elder of their offering.
237:
After comforting those merchants, he asked, "Where do you wish to go?" The merchants replied, "Venerable Sir, we wish to go only to our own place (the country of Sunāparanta)." The Elder stepped on a plank of the ship and made a determination: "Let it go to the place these people desire." When the merchants reached their own place, they told their wives and children about the matter and said, "Come, let us go to worship and attend upon the Elder." The five hundred merchants, together with their five hundred wives, established themselves in the Three Refuges and declared their status as lay followers.

Then, they unloaded the goods from the ship, made a portion for the Elder, and said, "Venerable Sir, this portion is for you." The Elder said, "I have no need for a separate portion. Have you ever seen the Teacher (the Buddha) before?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we have not," he said, "If so, with this portion of mine, construct a circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla) for the Teacher. In this way, you shall see the Teacher." The merchants said, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and began to construct the circular pavilion using both the Elder's portion and their own portions.

It is said that the Teacher made use of that circular pavilion from the time they began working on it. The guards, seeing the radiance at night, perceived, "There are powerful deities here." The lay followers completed the circular pavilion and the lodgings for the community of monks, prepared the offerings, and informed the Elder, "Venerable Sir, we have completed our task; please invite the Teacher." In the evening, the Elder went to Sāvatthī by psychic power and requested the Blessed One, "Venerable One, the lay followers living in Vāṇijagāma wish to see you; please show compassion to them." The Blessed One accepted. Knowing the Blessed One's acceptance, the Elder returned to his own place.

The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, tomorrow we shall wander for alms in the village of Vāṇijagāma in the country of Sunāparanta. Give the voting tickets (salāka) to four hundred and ninety-nine monks." The Elder replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and informed the community of monks, saying, "Let the monks who can travel through the air take the tickets." On that day, the Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna took the first ticket. The inhabitants of Vāṇijagāma, hearing that "The Teacher will come tomorrow," built a pavilion in the middle of the village and prepared an alms-hall.

Early in the morning, the Blessed One, after attending to his physical needs, entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) and sat down, attaining the fruition of meditative attainment (phalasamāpatti). The Sakka's Paṇḍukambala marble throne became hot. That Sakka, reflecting "Why is this?", saw that the Blessed One would be traveling to the country of Sunāparanta. He called the celestial architect Vissakamma and said, "Dear friend, today the Blessed One will wander for alms in a place three hundred leagues away. Create five hundred peaked mansions (pāsādas) and arrange them above the gateway of the Jetavana monastery for the journey." Vissakamma did as Sakka said. The mansion created for the Blessed One had four gateways. The mansions created for the two chief disciples had two gateways each. The mansions created for the remaining disciples had one gateway each. The Blessed One, having emerged from the Fragrant Chamber, among the mansions arranged in order...
238:
Sakka, having reflected and seen the Blessed One's journey to the Sunāparanta country, called the celestial craftsman Vissakamma and said, "Dear friend, today the Blessed One will wander for alms in a place three hundred yojanas away. Create five hundred peaked buildings (kūṭāgāras) and place them above the gate of Jetavana, prepared for travel." Vissakamma did as Sakka commanded. The Blessed One's peaked building had four entrances, those of the two chief disciples had two each, and the buildings for the remaining monks had one entrance each. The Blessed One emerged from the Gandhakuṭi and entered the foremost of the peaked buildings arranged in order. Led by the two chief disciples, four hundred and ninety-nine monks also went and sat in the peaked buildings. One peaked building remained empty. Then, the five hundred peaked buildings flew up into the sky.

The Blessed One reached the mountain named Saccabandha and caused the peaked building to stop in mid-air. On that mountain lived an ascetic named Saccabandha, who held wrong views and was teaching them to the multitude, having reached the pinnacle of gain and fame. Within him, the potential (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship shone like a lamp inside a jar. Seeing this, the Blessed One thought, "I shall preach the Dhamma to him," and went there to teach. At the end of the discourse, the ascetic attained the fruit of Arahantship; the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) came to him through the Path itself. He became an Ehi Bhikkhu and, carrying the robes and bowl created by psychic power, entered a peaked building.

The Blessed One, together with the five hundred monks in the peaked buildings, went to Vāṇija village. Having made the peaked buildings invisible, he entered the village. The merchants offered a great donation to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha and escorted the Blessed One to the Makulakārāma monastery. The Blessed One entered the circular hall (maṇḍalamāla). While the Blessed One was resting from the fatigue of the meal, the people ate their breakfast, undertook the Uposatha precepts, and returned to the monastery with many perfumes and flowers to listen to the Dhamma. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma. The multitude was released from their bonds, and a great Buddha-uproar (Buddhakolāhala) arose.

The Blessed One stayed in that village for two or three days to favor the people, but at dawn, he would always be at the Mahāgandhakuṭi. After staying there for a few days and wandering for alms in Vāṇija village, he sent Puṇṇa Thera back, saying, "You stay right here," and while on the way...
239:
There is a river named Nammadā; the Blessed One went to its bank. The Nammadā Naga King welcomed the Blessed One, invited him to the Naga realm, and made offerings to the Triple Gem. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the Naga King and then departed from the Naga realm. The Naga King requested, "Venerable Sir, please give me something to worship," so the Blessed One showed him a footprint shrine (pādacetitya) on the bank of the Nammadā River. That footprint is covered when the waves come and revealed when they recede; it became an object of great veneration.

The Blessed One departed from there and went to Saccabandha Mountain, where he said to the ascetic Saccabandha, "You have led many people down the path to the lower realms. Stay here, make them abandon their wrong views, and establish them on the path to Nibbāna." He too requested an object of worship. The Blessed One showed him a footprint shrine on a solid stone slab, as if a seal had been pressed into a lump of wet clay, and then returned to Jetavana. With reference to this meaning, the words beginning with "Tenevantara-vassena" were spoken.

"Parinibbāyi" means attaining Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). The people performed the funeral rites for the Thera's body for seven days, gathered much sandalwood, cremated the body, took the relics, and built a stupa (cetiya). "Sambahulā bhikkhū" refers to the monks who were present at the Thera's cremation site. All the remaining words are clear.

## 4. Nandakovāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth: this is the Nandakovāda Sutta. Therein, "tena kho pana samayena" means that the Blessed One, requested by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, sent away the community of nuns, assembled the community of monks, and assigned the responsibility to the Saṅgha, saying, "Let the elder monks exhort the nuns in rotation." This was spoken with reference to that assignment. Therein, "pariyāyena" means by turn or in rotation. "Na icchati" means that when his turn arrived, he would go to a distant village or start tasks like sewing, causing others to say, "This is the procrastination (papañca) of this elder." In truth, the Blessed One established this exhortation in rotation specifically because of the Elder Nandaka. Why? Because when these nuns saw the Elder, their minds became concentrated...
240:
Upon seeing the Venerable Nandaka, those nuns became composed and full of faith. Therefore, they desired to receive his instructions and listen to the Dhamma. For this reason, the Buddha thought, "Nandaka will give instructions and preach the Dhamma when his turn arrives," and thus assigned the instruction by turn. However, the Elder did not give instructions when it was his turn. Why did he not do so? It is said that in the past, when the Elder ruled as a king in Jambudīpa, those nuns had been his harem. Knowing this through his knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), the Elder thought: "If other monks who possess the knowledge of past lives see me sitting in the midst of this community of nuns (bhikkhunī-saṅgha), preaching the Dhamma using metaphors and logical reasons, they might observe this and think or say, 'Venerable Nandaka still cannot let go of his harem even today; this Venerable looks splendid surrounded by a retinue of concubines.'" Seeing this consequence clearly, the Elder did not give instructions on his turn. Knowing that only the teaching of that Elder would be suitable for these nuns, the Buddha called for the Venerable Nandaka.

The following story illustrates how those nuns had previously been the Elder's harem. Long ago in the city of Bārāṇasī, five hundred male slaves and five hundred female slaves—a total of one thousand people—worked together and lived in one place. At that time, this Venerable Nandaka was the head slave, and Gotamī was the head female slave. That head female slave was the wise and clever wife of the head slave. She would organize all one thousand people to act in unison when performing meritorious deeds. Then, at the time for entering the rains retreat (vassūpanāyika), five Paccekabuddhas came from the Nandamūlaka mountain glen to the Isipatana Migadāya forest. After wandering for alms in the city, they returned to Isipatana. Thinking, "We shall ask for manual labor to build huts (kuṭi) for the rains retreat," they donned their robes and entered the city in the evening, standing at the door of a merchant's house. While the head female slave was going to the water ghat carrying a pot, she saw the Paccekabuddhas entering the city. When the merchant heard the reason for the arrival of those Noble Ones, he said, "We have no opportunity; please proceed."

Then, the head female slave, who was entering while carrying her pot, saw those Noble Ones departing from the city. She set down her pot, paid homage, and asked with a bowed head, "Venerable sirs, you have only just entered the city; why are you leaving already?" They replied, "We came to ask for manual labor to build huts for the rains retreat." She asked, "Did you receive it, Bhante?" They replied, "We did not, lay follower." She then asked, "Venerable sirs, must these huts be built only by the powerful and wealthy? Can the poor not build them as well?" They replied, "Anyone can build them." She said, "Very well, Bhante, we shall build them. Please accept alms from me tomorrow."
241:
After inviting them and bringing water to her house, she took her pot again and returned to stand on the path to the water ghat. To every remaining female slave who arrived, she said, "Stay here for a moment." When all had arrived, she asked, "Mothers, do you wish to always perform the work of a slave for others, or do you wish to be free from slavery?" They replied, "Lady, we wish to be free this very day." She said, "If so, I have invited five Paccekabuddhas for tomorrow, as they did not receive manual labor for building huts. Have your husbands provide labor for one day." Those women agreed and, in the evening when their husbands returned from the forest, they informed them. The men also agreed and gathered at the door of the head slave's house.

Then the head female slave said to them, "Dear brothers, provide the gift of labor to the Paccekabuddhas tomorrow," and explained the benefits. She even threatened those who were unwilling with stern admonition until they agreed. The next day, after offering food to the Paccekabuddhas, she gave the signal to all the male slaves. They immediately entered the forest, gathered timber and bamboo materials, and organized themselves into groups of one hundred. They built one hut for each Paccekabuddha, complete with a walkway (caṅkamana) and other surroundings. They provided beds, stools, and pots for drinking and washing water. After obtaining a promise from the Paccekabuddhas to reside there for the three months of the rains retreat, they began the rotation of offering alms. If there was someone who could not afford to give on his turn, the head female slave would bring food from her own house and offer it. Having looked after them for the three months in this manner, the head female slave had each slave donate one cloth, resulting in five hundred thick cloths. She had those cloths exchanged and made into sets of triple robes (ticīvara) to offer to the five Paccekabuddhas. The Paccekabuddhas then departed at their convenience. Those one thousand slaves, having performed meritorious deeds together, were reborn in the celestial realm after they passed away.

Those five hundred women were reborn in the houses of those five hundred men from time to time; at other times, all the women were reborn in the household of the head slave's son. Furthermore, at one time, the son of the head slave passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn in a royal family. Those five hundred goddesses were also reborn into families of great wealth and came to the house of the one who had attained kingship. Wandering through Saṃsāra in this manner, they were reborn into the royal families of the cities of Koliya and Devadaha during the time of our Buddha.

Venerable Nandaka also ordained and attained Arahantship. When the daughter of the head female slave reached maturity, she was established in the position of the Chief Queen of King Suddhodana. The remaining princesses were their...
242:
Those princesses went to the houses of those princes. Their husbands, the five hundred princes, had ordained after hearing the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching during the dispute over water. The princesses sent messages to make those princes dissatisfied [with the holy life]. The Blessed One took those monks who were dissatisfied to Lake Kuṇāla, established them in the fruit of Stream-entry, and on the day of the Mahāsamaya Sutta, established them in the fruit of Arahantship. Those five hundred princesses also left the household life and ordained in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. The story of the Venerable Nandaka and these many bhikkhunīs should be understood in this way.

Rājakārāma refers to the monastery built and offered by King Pasenadi, located in the southern part of the city in a place similar to Thūpārāma.

'Sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ' means seen according to reality through insight wisdom with proper cause.

'Tajjaṃ tajjaṃ' refers to the nature that is the cause of that feeling. In terms of meaning, it means that those respective feelings arise depending on those respective causes.

'Pagevassa chāyā' means the shadow that arises depending on roots and so on is impermanent from the very beginning.

'Anupahacca' means without destroying (without harming). In butchering, one who makes the meat into lumps and lets the skin adhere is said to destroy the mass of flesh. One who makes the skin into joints and lets it adhere to the meat is also said to destroy the mass of flesh. [The text implies] doing it without such actions. 'Vilimaṃsanhārubandhanaṃ' refers only to the flesh adhering to the entire skin. 'Antarākilesasaṃyojanabandhanaṃ' is spoken with reference to all internal defilements.

Why was 'Satta kho panime' (Indeed, these seven) spoken? Because the path-wisdom that cuts defilements is not able to cut defilements by its own nature alone. Just as a hatchet cannot cut what is to be cut by its own nature but cuts only by depending on a man's effort, so too, path-wisdom cannot cut defilements without the six factors of enlightenment. Therefore, this was said. 'Tena hi' means because you [have shown] the six internal bases, the six...
243:
Having shown the six external bases, the six classes of consciousness, the simile of the lamp, the simile of the tree, and the simile of the butcher, the teaching was concluded with the seven factors of enlightenment leading to the destruction of the taints. For that reason, [the Buddha said,] "You should exhort those bhikkhunīs with that same exhortation tomorrow as well."

"That stream-enterer" refers to the one who was the very last among them in terms of spiritual qualities; she was a stream-enterer. The others, however, were once-returners, non-returners, and those who had destroyed the taints (Arahants). If that is so, why is it said "those with fulfilled aspirations"? It is because of the fulfillment of their intentions. For the bhikkhunī who thought, "If only I could realize the fruit of stream-entry right in this seat while listening to the Dhamma teaching of the Venerable Nandaka," she realized the fruit of stream-entry. For those who thought, "the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or Arahatship," they realized Arahatship. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "They were delighted and their aspirations were fulfilled."

## 5. Explanation of the Rāhulovāda Sutta

In the Rāhulovāda Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," "vimuttipāripācanīyā" means those that bring liberation (the fruit of Arahatship) to maturity; thus they are called "ripening for liberation." "Dhammā" refers to the fifteen qualities. These qualities should be understood as the causes for the purification of the faculty of faith and so on. It has been stated thus:

"The faculty of faith is purified by these three factors: avoiding faithless persons, associating with, following, and serving faithful persons, and reflecting on discourses that inspire confidence. The faculty of energy is purified by these three factors: avoiding lazy persons, associating with, following, and serving energetic persons, and reflecting on the Right Efforts. The faculty of mindfulness is purified by these three factors: avoiding unmindful persons, associating with, following, and serving mindful persons, and reflecting on the foundations of mindfulness."
244:
The faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is purified. The faculty of concentration is purified by these three means: avoiding persons who are not concentrated, associating with, following, and serving persons who are concentrated, and reflecting on the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha).

The faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is purified. The faculty of wisdom is purified by these three means: avoiding unwise persons, associating with, following, and serving wise persons, and reflecting on the subjects that are the domain of profound knowledge (such as the aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, and dependent origination). Thus, by these fifteen means—avoiding the five types of persons to be avoided, associating with, following, and serving the five types of persons to be associated with, and reflecting on the five groups of Suttas—these five faculties are purified (Paṭisambhidāmagga, I, 185).

There are also another fifteen factors that lead to the maturity of liberation: these five faculties beginning with faith (saddhā), the five perceptions that are part of penetration—namely, the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), the perception of suffering in what is impermanent (anicce dukkha-saññā), the perception of non-self in what is suffering (dukkhe anatta-saññā), the perception of abandonment (pahāna-saññā), and the perception of dispassion (virāga-saññā)—and the five factors beginning with good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) taught to the Elder Meghiya. As for the question, "At what time did this thought occur to the Blessed One?"—it occurred while He was surveying the world at the time of dawn.

"Many thousands of deities" refers to the very deities who made aspirations together with the Venerable Rāhula when he made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara during his time as the Naga King Pālita. Among those deities, some were earth-bound deities (bhūmaṭṭhaka), some were sky-bound (antalikkhaka), some were of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājika), some were born in the deva worlds, and some were born in the Brahma world. However, on this day, all of them gathered in one place in the Andhavana forest. Regarding the "Dhamma-eye" (dhamma-cakkhu), in the Upāliovāda Sutta and the Dīghanakha Sutta, it refers to the First Path. In the Brahmāyu Sutta, it refers to the three lower Fruits. In this Sutta, the four Paths and the four Fruits should be understood as the Dhamma-eye. This is because among those deities, some became Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), some Once-returners (sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (anāgāmī), and some Arahants (khīṇāsava). There is no defined limit to the number of those deities. The remaining words are clear in every respect.

## 6. Chachakka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Chachakka Sutta. Therein, "ādikalyāṇaṃ" means He will teach it making it good and faultless in the beginning. The same method applies to the middle and the end. In this way, the Blessed One praised the Ariyavaṃsa (Noble Lineage) with nine terms, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta with seven terms, and the Mahā-assapura Sutta with seven terms. However, He praised this Chachakka Sutta with nine terms.

"Veditabbāni" refers to the things to be known by the Path along with insight (vipassanā). By the mind-base (manāyatana), only the consciousness of the three planes (tebhūmaka-citta) is spoken of; by the phenomenon-base (dhammāyatana), the external phenomena of the three planes are also spoken of. By mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), excluding the ten sense-consciousnesses (dve-pañca-viññāṇa), the remaining twenty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness are spoken of. Contact (phassa) and feeling (vedanā) are only those associated with the aforementioned resultant consciousness. "Taṇhā" (craving) is the craving that arises at the moment of the impulsion (javana) with resultant feeling as its condition.

"The eye is self" (cakkhu attā) is a separate sequence (anusandhi). This teaching is undertaken to show the non-self nature of the two truths—Suffering and Origin—taught below. Therein, "na upappajjati" means it is not fitting/logical, and "veti" means it vanishes or ceases.

"But this, bhikkhus" (ayaṃ kho pana bhikkhave) is also a separate sequence. This teaching is undertaken to show the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) by means of the three graspings (gāha): craving, conceit, and views. They also say it is to show the round by means of the two truths: Suffering and Origin. In the phrases beginning with "this is mine" (etaṃ mama), only the graspings of craving, conceit, and views should be understood. "Samanupassati" means seeing by means of the three graspings.

Having thus shown the round, He now speaks the passage beginning with "But this..." (ayaṃ kho pana) to show the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) by means of the opposites of the three graspings, or by means of the two truths: Cessation and the Path. The words beginning with "this is not mine" (netaṃ mama) are words of negation for craving and so on. "Samanupassati" means seeing as impermanent, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta).

Having thus shown the ending of the round, He now speaks the passage beginning with "And the eye, bhikkhus" (cakkhuñca bhikkhave) to show the round again by means of the three underlying tendencies (anusaya). Therein, the words beginning with "he delights in" (abhinandati) are spoken only by means of craving and views. "Anuseti" means it remains unabandoned. "Dukkhassa" refers to the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements.
246:
Having thus taught the truth of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) by way of the three underlying tendencies (anusaya), now, wishing to show the truth of the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) by way of their opposites, He spoke the words beginning with 'Cakkhuñca' again. 'Having abandoned ignorance' (avijjāṃ pahāya) means having abandoned ignorance, which is the root of the cycle. 'Knowledge' (vijjāṃ) means having brought about the wisdom associated with the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga).

The phrase 'This situation exists' (ṭhānametaṃ vijjati) means that the Blessed One, having brought the teaching to a conclusion by way of the cycle and its cessation through this sequence of discourse, and wishing to show that same truth collectively once more, spoke the words beginning with 'Thus seeing, bhikkhus' (evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave). In the phrase 'about sixty monks' (saṭṭhimattānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ), the meaning should be understood thus: It is not surprising that sixty monks reached the Fruit of Arahatship while the Tathāgata Himself was teaching. Even when the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), Venerable Sāriputta Thera, taught this Chachakka Sutta, sixty monks reached the Fruit of Arahatship. Likewise, when Venerable Mahāmoggallāna taught it, and when the Eighty Great Elders (asītimahāthera) taught it, sixty monks reached the Fruit of Arahatship in each case. This too is not surprising, for those disciples were ones who had attained great supernormal powers (mahābhiññā).

However, in later times, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, an elder named Māleyyadeva Thera taught this Chachakka Sutta beneath the Lohapāsāda (Brazen Palace). At that time too, sixty monks reached the Fruit of Arahatship. Just as he taught at the Lohapāsāda, the elder also taught this sutta at the Mahāmaṇḍapa. Leaving the Mahāvihāra, he went to Cetiyapabbata and taught there as well. Then he taught at Sakiyavaṃsa Monastery, Kūṭāli Monastery, Antarasobbha, Muttaṅgaṇa, Vātakapabbata, Pācinagharaka, Dīghavāpi, Lokandara, and Nomaṇဍalatala. In each of those places, sixty monks reached the Fruit of Arahatship.

Furthermore, the elder departed from there and went to Cittalapabbata. At that time, there was a Great Elder at Cittalapabbata Monastery who had over sixty years of seniority (vassa). There was a secluded spot in a pond called Kuruvakatittha, where the Great Elder went down to bathe. Māleyyadeva Thera went to him and said, 'Venerable sir, let me bathe you.' The Great Elder, out of courtesy, thought, 'They say there is an elder named Māleyyadeva; this must be him,' and asked, 'Are you [Māleyyadeva] Deva?' He replied, 'Yes, venerable sir.' The elder said, 'Friend, for the sixty years of my monkhood, no one has ever touched my body with their hands. You, however, may bathe me.' He then came out of the water and sat on the bank.

Māleyyadeva Thera performed all the duties, such as rubbing the hands and feet, and bathed the Great Elder. That day was also a day for hearing the Dhamma. Then the Great Elder said, 'Friend Māleyyadeva, it is proper for you to give us the gift of Dhamma.' The elder accepted, saying, 'Very well, venerable sir.' At sunset...
247:
At sunset, the call for hearing the Dhamma was made. Sixty Great Elders, all with over sixty years of seniority, came to hear the Dhamma. Deva Thera (Māleyyadeva) began this sutta (Chachakka Sutta) at the conclusion of the melodic recitation (sarabhañña), and at the end of the sutta, the sixty Great Elders reached the Fruit of Arahatship. Then he went to Tissamahāvihāra and taught; there too, sixty elders [reached the Fruit of Arahatship]. Then he taught at Nāgamahāvihāra in Kāḷakaccha village; there too, sixty elders [reached the Fruit of Arahatship]. Then he went to Kalyāṇī and taught beneath the palace on the fourteenth day; there too, sixty elders [reached the Fruit of Arahatship]. On the Uposatha day, he taught above the palace; there too, sixty elders [reached the Fruit of Arahatship]. Thus, while Deva Thera himself was teaching this sutta, sixty people (monks) reached the Fruit of Arahatship in each of sixty locations.

However, at Ambilakāḷaka Vihāra, when Tipitaka Cūḷanāga Thera taught this sutta, the human audience extended for a quarter-league (gāvuta), and the celestial audience for a league (yojana). At the end of the sutta, a thousand monks reached the Fruit of Arahatship, while among the deities, only one worldling (puthujjana) remained here and there.
